#9875. Exception Best Practices

Good exception handling is difficult in any language, but all the more so in Haskell, where asynchronous exceptions mean that code can be interrupted at almost any point. In this blog post we will discuss a series of recommendations, focusing on three goals:

As we will see, satisfying all three of these goals together can be tricky, and sometimes they are in direct tension.

This is part one of our series on exceptions.

Part 1: Exception best practices (this blog post)

Part 2: âWhen an interruptible call isnât interruptibleâ, which will be published soon, discusses interruptible foreign calls: how they are meant to work, why they do not always work, and how to address that.

Part 3: â(Some) Exceptions in Haskell are resumableâ, also to be published soon, discusses asynchronous exceptions in pure code, resulting in resumable exceptions, and how we might generalize that to IO code.

Weâre also still planning two further parts: one on composing masking operations, and one exploring how the problems discussed in part 3 can be resolved.

In this first section we recap the most important concepts that we will need to understand before we can discuss best practices.

An exception is thrown with throwIO and caught with catch; in both cases the type of the value that is thrown must be an instance of the Exception class:

It is often more convenient to use handle, which is just catch with its arguments flipped:

Before throwIO can throw the exception, it must first wrap it in the SomeException envelope, which carries dynamic typing information and exception annotations:

This dynamic typing information is used by catch to ensure that only exceptions of the desired type are caught (that is, determined by the type of the exception handler).

Synchronous exceptions are exceptions that are raised as a direct consequence of executing the program itself. Haskell also supports asynchronous exceptions, which instead can occur at any point during execution1. Consider the following example:

It might seem that the handler should never run, but that is not necessarily the case:

If throwIO is the prototypical way to throw a synchronous exception, throwTo is its asynchronous sibling, and throws an exception to an arbitrary thread, although in practice it is rarely called directly; instead, it is a building block for other abstractions:

Without asynchronous exceptions, none of this would be possible in general: the code being cancelled would have to check, at regular intervals, whether it should stop.

Consider this code that attempts to read the first line of a file; it tries to make sure that the file handle is closed again if an exception is raised during reading:

The problem in this code is in between the lines; specifically, after the openFile and before the catch. The solution is to temporarily prevent asynchronous exceptions from being raised using mask, and only enable them again once we are safely in the scope of an exception handler:

The pattern in readFirstLineLOWLEVEL is so common in Haskell that it has its own combinator, called bracket; it takes three arguments, one to acquire a resource, one to release it again, and then the body that uses the resource. This means that the recommended, and idiomatic, way to write readFirstLine is

One downside of this idiom is that the exception handler no longer gets access to the exception. For example, if we wanted to log any exceptions that occurred while we were reading the file, along with the position in the file when the exception was thrown, we would not be able to do so with the standard bracket. It is of course always possible to drop back down to the low-level mask combinator, but in most cases it is probably better to instead use generalBracket from the exceptions package. When using generalBracket, the handler is told how the body terminated, and can also produce a result of its own (returned only on successful termination2).

(The reason for the fmap is that generalBracket allows the deallocation callback to return an additional value; here we just ignore it.)

Consider this version of readFirstLine that tries again when an exception happens; perhaps the file weâre trying to read might be locked by another process, and we just want to keep trying until we succeed:

Code like this with a blanket exception handler that catches all exceptions (by catching exceptions of type SomeException) is problematic. The obvious problem is that while some synchronous exceptions might be transient (âfile lockedâ), others might not (âinvalid pathâ); you probably donât want to retry on the latter. The less obvious problem is that you almost certainly donât want to retry on asynchronous exceptions at all: exceptions such as a Timeout or UserInterrupt (CTRL-C) should almost certainly be honoured.

Consider this variation of keepTrying; unlike in the previous section, weâre now specifically only re-trying if the file is locked, but we have a different error:

The problem with this version is that since the recursion happens inside of the exception handler, we might end up with an unbounded number of handlers, each next recursive call running under all of the exception handlers installed so far. In the previous section keepTryingBAD did get this aspect right: return a value that indicates whether or not we should retry, so that we can retry outside the scope of the exception handler.

Consider the following code, which spawns an auxiliary thread which catches all exceptions, and then shows that exception using anythingToString from my recover-rtti package, which bypasses any kind of Show instance (indeed, any type class instance at all) and shows the exact structure of the exception:

When we run this, we see (slightly cleaned up for readability, and some details omitted):

The outermost wrapper is SomeException, with the dynamic typing information (TrTyCon ..) and the (empty) list of exception annotations (ExceptionContext []), which we already mentioned above, and the innermost constructor ThreadKilled is the exception itself. However, we additionally have another wrapper in between: SomeAsyncException.

This wrapper serves as a marker for async exceptions. It is not an indication of how the exception was delivered (synchronously or asynchronously), and this is as it should be: the marker indicates intent (âthis exception was raised because of external circumstances, rather than the code itselfâ). Asynchronous exceptions are often caught and then rethrown synchronously (for example, see the section about bracket), which changes the delivery mechanism but not the intent.3

This does however mean that this intent must be stated explicitly. For example, in our first example of asynchronous exceptions we asynchronously threw MyException to another thread, without ever wrapping MyException in SomeAsyncException. If MyException was intended to be used asynchronously, we should use a custom Exception instance:4

Conversely, we can test if something is an async exception by checking for the wrapper:

In general, it is good practice to ensure that code that might wait for an unbounded amount of time, such as when acquiring a lock, can always be cancelled, for example through a timeout or through CTRL-C (UserInterrupt). Iâm intentionally using cancellability instead of âinterruptibilityâ, since the latter has a very specific technical meaning in Haskell, as we shall discuss now.

Note. Foreign calls in Haskell (safe or unsafe) are not cancellable. Alongside safe and unsafe there are also interruptible foreign calls, which we will discuss in part 2 of this blog post series on exceptions. The term interruptible, when applied to foreign calls, is related to, but not the same as, the âinterruptible operationsâ we discuss here.

When we discussed bracket, we glossed over one detail: it does not unmask exceptions when it invokes the acquire callback to acquire the resource, nor when it invokes the release callback to release it again. This is a thorny subject that we have written about before (Dealing with Asynchronous Exceptions during Resource Acquisition); here we highlight the two most important concepts only.

First, even with async exceptions masked, interruptible operations can still receive exceptions; paraphrasing the paper slightly: âAny operation which may need to wait indefinitely for a resource may receive asynchronous exceptions even within an enclosing mask, but only while the resource is unavailableâ. The canonical example is takeMVar, which can receive exceptions as long as it hasnât managed to take the MVar yet, making a pattern such as this safe:

will still be able to interrupt the takeMVar. Unfortunately, interruptibility is not visible from a functionâs type, and is typically not even documented; for example, putStrLn is interruptible (because deep down its bowels it calls takeMVar somewhere on the MVar buried inside a Handle), which means that this variation on withLock is broken:

The presence of putStrLn essentially pokes a hole in the careful masked state that bracket provides: if an asynchronous exception arrives after the takeMVar succeeds but before the putStrLn, the exception can be thrown (if there is contention for that handle MVar), and the putMVar will never run, leaving the lock forever unusable. A good intuition is to keep acquire and release as simple as possible; in the next few sections we will study some more involved cases.

When acquiring multiple resources, it is important that we either acquire all of them or none of them (atomicity). This means we need to worry about previously acquired resources when we get (synchronous or asynchronous) exceptions while acquiring more. The easiest option is to nest bracket:

Sometimes however the specific way that resources must be acquired and released does not allow for simple lexical scoping like this; or perhaps only offering a âwithâ (bracket) style API is too limiting at call sites. If you need to provide an API that acquires multiple resources, you have to think about how to deal with the presence of interruptible operations; for example, you might do something like

There is no point calling mask inside of takeMVars, because if the enclosing context does not have exceptions masked, then leaving the scope of that inner mask could result in an async exception being delivered at that point.

In general this can be quite tricky to get right, and it is often better to try and avoid solving this problem at all. For the case of MVar-like resources, the obvious alternative is to use TMVars instead, and just take both TMVars inside a single transaction.

If you must release multiple resources, you should ensure that if one resource fails to release cleanly and throws an exception, you still release the remainder; one option is to chain using finally:

In the standard bracket acquire release body pattern, if release fails with an exception, but it itself was invoked because of an exception in body, itâs debatable which exception should be propagated. For current GHC versions the exception from release is propagated, but starting with GHC 10.0, the choice is dissolved entirely: the exception from release will be propagated with a WhileHandling annotation of the original exception.

We will consider async exceptions during release a bit further down.

It is also possible to mask exceptions so that even interruptible operations can no longer receive exceptions by using uninterruptibleMask instead of mask:

This is safer in the sense that the takeMVar mb cannot throw an exception, but less safe because this code is now no longer cancellable: timeouts, user-interrupts (CTRL-C) etc. will not have any effect. To solve that youâd have to poll: explicitly check whether any async exceptions are waiting to be delivered, for example using unsafeUnmask (allowInterrupt, which does exactly this under mask, has no effect under uninterruptibleMask).

Another, possibly simpler, option to create an uninterruptible operation is to fork an auxiliary thread to do the resource acquisition. Since this thread is private, it is essentially immune to async exceptions.5 However, this will then still require some kind of communication protocol that allows the child thread to clean up when it realizes the parent is no longer interested; see also the discussion of Threads, below.

The ability to cancel code is often more important during resource acquisition than it is during release; acquiring a lock can take an unbounded amount of time, but releasing the lock does not. However, sometimes releasing a resource can take an unbounded amount of time also. Perhaps releasing the resource literally is acquiring a lock, perhaps to modify some kind of worker pool:

Or perhaps the resource is a connection to a server and disconnecting requires some kind of closing handshake to ensure an orderly closure (e.g.Â TLS uses closure alerts to avoid truncation attacks):

In this case, all the same considerations apply as during resource acquisition: the release callback is invoked with async exceptions masked, but interruptible operations can still receive exceptions.

In some cases you may want to vary what the resource release function does, depending on whether or not the body terminated with an exception, and depending on the nature of that exception (see also discussion of generalBracket). For example, you may (or may not) opt for an abortive closure of a TLS connection after a timeout; or you may (or may not) opt to close a file handle without flushing the buffer. Such decisions are of course highly application specific; a timeout may simply mean that the main action should be terminated, but the resource should still be closed cleanly!

Threads are a microcosm of the three goals that we set up at the start of this blog post: we must avoid leaking threads, communication between threads can get stuck, and exceptions thrown in threads often need to be dealt with outside of those threads.

New threads run with an exception handler that silently swallows the asynchronous ThreadKilled, as well as synchronous BlockedIndefinitelyOnMVar and BlockedIndefinitelyOnSTM, which we will revisit shortly. Any other exception is handled by the uncaught exception handler, which by default simply prints it (though this can be changed).

In general it is good practice to ensure no exception is ever uncaught.6 In almost all cases you should therefore install an exception handler in the new thread; what this handler should do will be application specific, but we will consider one important class of problems in the next section.

Consider a producer and consumer thread that communicate through a buffered interface such as an MVar:

The MVar provides back-pressure, which is good: the producer canât race ahead and produce an unbounded number of chunks if the consumer is not consuming them. However, if the producer aborts with an exception, the consumer will be left waiting for the next chunk which will never arrive.

There are a number of ways to deal with this. Probably my favourite is to record the exception in the buffer itself; this means that the consumer is forced to consider what to do when the producer fails:

Note that catching all exceptions here is correct: the consumer wants to know if the producer disappeared, even if that was because of an async exception.

Another option, arguably more compositional, is to use STM, and record the health of the producer separately from the consumer:

If you choose this route, it is important to read both variables in a single atomically block, to ensure that when the transaction is blocked waiting for a chunk, it will be retried either when a new chunk becomes available or when the health of the producer changes.

If you donât signal failure in the producer in any way to the consumer, the consumer may fail with a âblocked indefinitely on MVarâ or âblocked indefinitely on STMâ exception. You should regard this strictly as a debugging tool only, in the same category as Debug.Trace. Do not rely on it for your program logic: false negatives are common (where the exception is not raised even though code might be blocked indefinitely), and if you ever catch it, then false positives are possible (where code is not blocked indefinitely and yet the exception is raised).

New threads are spawned with forkIO, and inherit the masking state from their parent. We can take advantage of this fact to start a thread which starts with exceptions already masked.

Consider the producer thread example we saw earlier. A naive attempt to spawn a new producer might look like this:

If the producer is spawned in this manner, but is killed before it installs the exception handler, the consumer will be left waiting forever. For example, the caller of newProducerBROKEN is given the ThreadId, so it may kill the producer before the forked thread is ever scheduled. Masking asynchronous exceptions from within the thread cannot help here: the exception might arrive before we get a chance to call mask. Instead we must fork the thread with exceptions already masked, by masking them in the parent thread.

However, we cannot use the normal mask function; the restore function that it gives us will restore the masking state to what it was prior to the call to mask; we instead want to ensure that the new thread really runs with exceptions unmasked, independent of what the masking state in the parent was. Function forkIOWithUnmask gives us precisely this:

Note that there is a function in base that captures nearly this pattern: forkFinally. However, forkFinally does not use forkIOWithUnmask, but uses a regular mask, making it more sensitive to the masking state of the thread in which it is invoked; in particular, you almost certainly donât want to call forkFinally inside the acquire callback of bracket (see also Bracketing thread creation below).

To kill a thread, you use throwTo to throw a ThreadKilled to the target thread; this is such a common idiom, base provides killThread that does exactly this.

An important aspect of throwTo is that it is synchronous: it does not return until the exception has been raised in the target thread. This can be convenient; for example, consider a networking context in which we want to send a timeout message after a certain period:

The parent thread is guaranteed that the child thread wonât send the notification anymore after the killThread, without the need for any explicit synchronization with the child thread. It also has some downsides, however, as we shall see in the next section.

Threads are a resource like any other, and we should ensure that they get cleaned up. It is tempting to write

Both the acquire and the release of this example are wrong. First, as we saw above, when we fork a new thread it inherits the masking state from its parent. Since bracket runs the acquire callback with exceptions masked, this means that the new thread will now run with async exceptions masked at all times (modulo unsafeUnmask). However, even if we fix this by using forkIOWithUnmask instead, there is still a problem:

We saw above that throwTo is synchronous: it waits until the exception is delivered to the child thread, which means it must wait until the child thread can receive async exceptions. Because it might have to wait, it is interruptible; and unlike takeMVar, which is interruptible only if the MVar is not available, throwTo is always interruptible. This means that if this bracket itself is executed by a thread that is killed, we might not clean up the auxiliary thread. This is therefore an example of where the use of uninterruptibleMask_ is really justified:

This does mean that the parent thread (the one running this bracket) will be cancellable only if the child thread is too; an unjustified use of uninterruptibleMask_ in the child thread (the orderly closure example we discussed above), resulting in uncancellable child threads, propagates and results in uncancellable parent threads.

In this blog post we focused mostly on principles, not the larger ecosystem. We cannot possibly give an exhaustive overview here, but there are a few packages that we should briefly discuss. Two I can unreservedly recommend: exceptions and async. The third, safe-exceptions, takes an opinionated stance on async exceptions which you may or may not want to adopt; here we will only point out some aspects to be aware of.

The exceptions package provides polymorphic versions of the standard exception handling functions through a stack of type classes: MonadThrow for monads in which we can throw exceptions, MonadCatch in which we can catch them, and finally MonadMask in which we have bracket available. Itâs mostly a straight-forward generalization of the functions in base, with the exception of generalBracket, which we discussed already.

As we saw when we discussed threads, dealing correctly with threads is non-trivial, and async aims to make this better. It takes care of the following things:

Be aware, however, that cancelling a thread (implicitly through leaving the scope of withAsync, or explicitly through cancel), doesnât just kill the child thread, but waits for it to terminate. That can be important: if the parent and the child thread shared any resources, the parent can be sure that the child will not need them anymore. However, there are also cases where the parent does not need to, or perhaps even should not, wait for the child.

If you donât want to use withAsync, some of the old problems come back:

As mentioned, safe-exceptions takes an opinionated stance on async exceptions, which is provided through a series of alternative implementations of standard base functions: catch, bracket, throwTo and others all behave subtly differently in safe-exceptions than they do elsewhere. As such, if you choose to use this package, my strong recommendation is to import the package qualified, so that use sites (Safe.catch) are clearly distinguished from the standard functions.

The use of safe-exceptions should be a deliberate choice: it is not a drop-in replacement. Refactoring existing code to import from Control.Exception.Safe instead of Control.Exception, without making additional changes, is unlikely to be correct.

The first important difference is that Safe.catch and related functions do not allow you to catch async exceptions at all. This means that you donât have to worry about catching async exceptions in handlers that catch âallâ exceptions, though you probably should not do that anyway. If you do try to catch an async exception, the code will compile just fine, but the handler will never run.

In the section on distinguishing sync and async exceptions, we discussed that the difference is about intent, not delivery mechanism. We implied, though did not spell it out, that this intent is stated statically, through the Exception instance. However, in the implementation of throwTo in safe-exceptions this intent is stated dynamically: throwTo will add an AsyncExceptionWrapper around the exception being thrown if toException does not already add the SomeAsyncException wrapper. This gives a catcher the ability to still see that it was âintended to be asynchronousâ, but it also means that even if that catcher is defined using standard catch, and it has a handler for that exact exception, it wonât be able to catch it anymore because the type match will fail.7

The behaviour of Safe.bracket is also subtly different from standard bracket. The most important difference is that it wraps the release callback in uninterruptibleMask_. This means that the release callback does not need to worry about async exceptions, but as we saw in the section on async exceptions during release, this may not always be safer: in the network example, uninterruptibleMask_ around an orderly closure could mean that the code will wait indefinitely for the network peer to respond, and cannot be timed out or interrupted with CTRL-C.

The other difference in bracket is what happens when the release callback was called because of an exception in the body: depending on the exact nature of the two exceptions (sync or async), exceptions thrown by the release may be silently swallowed, making it all the more important to be careful if youâre releasing multiple resources.

Writing code that does the right thing even when things go wrong can be quite difficult; this is inherent, not accidental, complexity. Asynchronous exceptions make this significantly more difficult still, but of course also come with a lot of benefits; for example, without asynchronous exceptions a general combinator such as timeout would not be possible. Exceptions also tend to be non-deterministic, so leaked resources, stuck code, or unhandled failures may not be noticed during testing. Nonetheless, with some good code hygiene many problems can be avoided; hopefully the guidelines in this blog post can assist.

There are a few topics that we have not covered in this blog post:

Many thanks to Anduril for sponsoring this work.

The main reference here is Asynchronous Exceptions in Haskell by Marlow et al.â©ï¸

In addition to successful termination and abnormal termination with an exception, generalBracket also has a case for abnormal termination in monad stacks such as ExceptT. Since these are not strictly speaking exceptions, we will not discuss this any further in this blog post.â©ï¸

There are reasons to avoid synchronously rethrowing asynchronous exceptions; see GHC #2558, #24189 and #26368; however, those reasons are mostly orthogonal to our discussion here.â©ï¸

For the general mechanism at work here, see An Extensible Dynamically-Typed Hierarchy of Exceptions.â©ï¸

It would not be immune to async exceptions such as heap overflow, of course, but they are generally irrecoverable anyway. Strictly speaking it is not truly private either, as listThreads can be used to enumerate all threads.â©ï¸

The only technical exception to this is exitFailure, which should only be called from the main thread, and will throw an ExitCode exception.â©ï¸

Arguably, asynchronously throwing an exception with an Exception instance that does not use asyncExceptionToException and asyncExceptionFromException is a bug, but itâs probably a common one: simply deriving Exception is an easy mistake to make.â©ï¸

#9874. Bill for Birmingham's Oracle debacle reaches £128M

True cost may be much higher for delayed SAP replacement that helped bankrupt the city

Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse.

Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF].

The report, from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million.

The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues.

"The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said.

It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software.

The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems.

Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts. It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor. The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt, an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system.

It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless.

The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay, now rebranded as Civica Income Management.

Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill.

For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools, but that was excluded from the reimplementation.

Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example.

A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026.

Council taxpayers can be assured the new system has gone live without major problems, but that is hardly cause for celebration. ®

#9872. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#9870. Smartphone shipments face another bleak year before modest 2028 comeback

Counterpoint forecasts another 6% shipment drop in 2027, with volumes still below 2025 levels by decade's end

Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028.

That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker, which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers.

The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market.

Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns.

The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC, memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing.

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones.

Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported, memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026.

For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases.

"The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang.

"Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets."

Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years.

Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing.

A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery.

"The unusually low 2027 base creates the potential for a robust rebound in 2028 once the memory bottleneck begins to ease. But this should not be interpreted as a return to the old market trajectory," Wang said.

"Some low-end demand has been permanently lost, and the 2028 market will still be about 14 percent below 2025 shipments."

Potential availability of 6G-capable smartphones toward the end of the decade could give the market a boost, but Counterpoint does not expect it to regain its 2025 shipment levels by 2030. ®

#9869. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

4-step MiniMax-H3 — video with a matching soundtrack

Automatic1111-style studio on one gr.Workflow canvas

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

#9868. Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...]

Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository.

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It says two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.
