#9803. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:

The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#9802. Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At least 178 organizations, including several major brands, unwittingly exposed website visitors to hydra-like malware via a third-party platform.

Some of the world's most recognizable brands unwittingly became conduits for malware this week, after an attacker slipped malicious code into website testing scripts delivered by Optimizely, a platform that allows organizations to experiment with and optimize their online presence.

The attack potentially exposed visitors to sites operated by at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA — to malware capable of stealing payment card details, hijacking cryptocurrency transactions, and delivering exploit kits for iPhones and iPads.

Many organizations use Optimizely to run website experiments, test different page designs and personalize content for visitors. To do this, Optimizely embeds scripts in customer websites that can serve different versions of a page or its content to visitors, track their interactions, and measure which versions perform best.

Related:Matters.AI Lands India’s Largest Cybersecurity Pre-Series A Round to Fight AI Data Risks

The attackers appear to have exploited this mechanism to insert malicious code into a custom field called Project JavaScript, which allows Optimizely customers to run their own code across website pages.

British Web security monitoring service Report URI, among the first to detect the activity, documented the tampering but said it could not determine how the attackers gained the ability to modify customer projects. "We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain," Report URL founder Scott Helme wrote.

Report URI said it located and examined 1,611 unique Optimizely scripts. It found malicious code in 188 scripts associated with 178 organizations. The company has published a list of the affected websites on its site, grouped by industry sector.

Optimizely itself has said little about the incident so far besides acknowledging it and pinning it somewhat vaguely to a vulnerability in the platform's Experimentation account sign-up flow. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

In a follow-up statement to Dark Reading, Optimizely spokesperson identified these measures as including "blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts." The company has also implemented "additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation," the statement read. Optimizely however, did not respond to a Dark Reading question on how a vulnerability in the account sign-up flow could have given an attacker write access to customer projects.

"That’s the question every affected customer should be putting to Optimizely right now," says Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. "They need to know how a new account got write access to other tenants' projects, which project IDs were changed and when, and whether that path is fully closed."

Until Optimizely explains the authorization failure, customers can't judge whether the company's reported fix addresses the cause or just the symptom, he says.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

The incident is a reminder that organizations need strict controls over third-party scripts running on their websites, Beals adds. Most organizations approve a third-party vendor script once during procurement and never revisit it later. Optimizely, for instance, passed whatever review the 178 affected companies ran, and the malicious code still shipped from Optimizely's own CDN under its own certificate.

"The takeaway is that a vendor approval is a point-in-time decision, and the risk changes every time that vendor’s code changes," Beals says. "You can keep using these tools if you decide where they’re allowed to run."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, says incidents like these show why organizations implement a browser security feature called Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify that externally hosted files, such as JavaScript, haven't been altered before they are loaded and executed.

"The problem that we have here is that you may include a file in your website that is safe for months or even years and then, unbeknownst to you, a breach occurs within your vendor and that 'file that's been safe forever' is suddenly no longer safe," Reguly says.

SRI allows organizations to perform version pinning based on file hashes to protect against attacks like the one that went down at Optimizely. "The downside is that it requires a bit more effort and management to maintain your Web pages, which are often seen as 'set it and forget it' resources," Reguly adds.

Chris Nyhuis, CEO of Vigilant, says Optimizely demonstrates what happens when trust becomes an attack surface. "Organizations allowed a third party to deliver executable code into their customers' browsers, and that trust was exploited," he says.

The answer isn't to eliminate third-party technology but to eliminate "blind trust," Nyhuis says. "Restrict where vendor scripts execute, limit their access to sensitive data, monitor their behavior and changes, and independently validate what they're doing."

Furthermore, Optimizely also needs to explain how a flaw in an account sign-up process allowed an attacker to modify executable code belonging to 178 unrelated customers. "For that to happen, there had to be a path around customer authorization boundaries," he says. "Whether that involved broken tenant isolation, privilege escalation, an authorization flaw, or access to an overly privileged service remains to be established by the forensic investigation."

This article was updated at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 18 to reflect a statement from Optimizely.

#9801. Objections to .php application being published on ICANN site

After Automattic's confirmation that they would switch their .vibe application to the replacement string of .php1, ICANN has started to publish various objections on the Application Comment Forum (ACF) section of their new gTLD program site2. They mostly relate to the confusion and security risk posed by a common filetype (especially in web development) becoming a TLD, similar to the outcry over Google's application for .zip (which was eventually successfully delegated). The other common theme is the objection to a private company effectively trying to claim what is an open-source project.

The first is by PHP developer Larry Garfield who accused the WordPress parent of "Inappropriate Squatting":3

WordPress contributor Jamie VanRaalte objected on the grounds of "Part of a pattern - .php should not go to one company" and also said the .wordpress application was a similarly inappropriate power grab of another open-source project:4

Web developer Ryan Maietta highlighted the "File Extension Confusion and Security Risks" of using an established filetype as a TLD and the risk of people confusing websites using this domain as being officially endorsed by the PHP project:5

Forensic analyst Herbert Bärschneider also objected simply on the grounds of confusing the TLD with the filetype:6

And finally, the ICANN-affiliated Mark William Datysgeld described .php as being "Not viable from a technical perspective"7 highlighting that he has already had issues creating the page for it on the PHP-based ICANN Wiki site, causing it to return a 404 error response8:

Testing out a simple blogging method because I'm excited about the new gTLD program 2026 round and what that means for all the silly new domain possibilities for fedi instances and bsky handles. Silly articles at https://bld.roddie.digital.

#9800. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors

Nov 27, 2026 21 min read

A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.

Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.

However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.

Microsoft Ignite 2026; Explore What's Next in AI and Software Engineering - Learn how to architect agentic systems, modernize cloud infrastructure, and tackle emerging engineering challenges. Get practical insights from Microsoft experts and industry leaders. Watch on demand.

In fact, a GPS update may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.

Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.

I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.

This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.

For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.

For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.

For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.

For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.

The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.

I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.

This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.

I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.

A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image shows. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.

Figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author)

Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.

A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.

Why preserve the original? Because a later transformation may be incorrect, an assumption may change, or an event may be disputed. If the system retains only its normalized output, engineers may be unable to determine whether the original observation was poor or the transformation introduced the error.

For example, suppose an application converts a GPS speed reading into a standardized unit and later combines it with vehicle speed. If an event looks implausible, the engineering team should be able to inspect the original value, its timestamp, and the conversion applied to it.

Sensor streams do not necessarily report at the same frequency or on the same schedule. A vehicle interface may produce frequent speed updates while GPS observations arrive less often. Mobile and backend components may also introduce different buffering and delivery delays.

The first distinction I make is between measurement time and arrival time.

Measurement time describes when the observation was captured, according to its source clock. Arrival time describes when a component received it. Arrival time is useful for understanding latency, but it is not a safe substitute for measurement time when reconstructing physical events.

A stream processor that compares the latest values received from two sources can accidentally compare different moments. This becomes especially problematic during rapid acceleration, braking, or turning, when the underlying state changes quickly.

The architecture should therefore define an alignment policy. It needs to specify how observations are matched, how much temporal separation is acceptable for each use case, and what happens when the system cannot find a suitable match.

Interpolation may be appropriate for some continuous signals, but it should not be applied indiscriminately. It can create a plausible-looking value where the evidence is sparse, and it may obscure a sharp change. The system should retain whether a value was directly measured, interpolated, or otherwise estimated.

When alignment cannot be established within the required tolerance, the right result may be lower confidence or no event at all.

A measurement's value is only part of its meaning. Its unit, coordinate frame, source, and interpretation matter just as much.

A phone's accelerometer reports motion in device coordinates. Those axes are attached to the phone, not inherently to the vehicle. If the phone rotates in a mount, the relationship between the phone's axes and the vehicle's forward, lateral, and vertical directions changes.

A system that assumes the phone is always mounted in the same orientation can interpret device movement as vehicle movement. That can distort acceleration, braking, and turning estimates.

Normalization should make these assumptions explicit. It may include unit conversion, coordinate transformation, sensor calibration, and checks on the validity of orientation estimates. A transformed observation should retain enough information to identify the transformation and its assumptions.

The system must also distinguish coordinate normalization from measurement quality. A transformation can be mathematically correct but based on an uncertain orientation estimate. The result may therefore remain unsuitable for a particular event calculation.

At this stage, the system asks a different question: not simply whether a value exists, but whether it is fit for the intended use.

Useful checks include freshness, timestamp alignment, missing samples, source consistency, measurement uncertainty, and the reliability of any required coordinate transformation.

These checks should not be buried inside individual event rules. A shared quality stage gives different event detectors a consistent view of the evidence and makes quality decisions easier to monitor and test.

These are not universal labels with fixed thresholds. A GPS observation might be adequate for a coarse trip map but unsuitable for calculating a short, sharp braking event. Quality must be evaluated in context.

Event detection should consume measurements that have already passed through the relevant quality checks.

This does not mean every event requires every sensor. A trip-start detector and a harsh-braking detector have different evidence requirements. The architecture should allow each detector to declare what it needs and how it handles missing or uncertain inputs.

Consider a braking detector that combines vehicle speed and GPS speed. If the two values refer to different moments, the detector may infer a rate of deceleration that is not supported by the underlying movement. A quality-aware design prevents the detector from treating a poor match as equivalent to aligned observations.

The detector should also distinguish the event's classification from the quality of its evidence. An event may be a candidate for further review rather than a definitive result. Keeping these concepts separate makes the system easier to tune without changing the meaning of quality checks throughout the pipeline.

The final stage produces more than an event label.

A useful event record can include the event type, event time or interval, relevant vehicle or trip association, quality status, supporting observations, and the processing-rule version. Where a confidence estimate is used, its meaning and limitations should be documented rather than treating it as a universal probability of correctness.

This information makes a decision inspectable. An engineer can trace an event to the observations that supported it, see whether any measurements were downgraded, and understand which processing logic was applied.

It also helps separate two questions that are often conflated: "What did the system decide?" and "What evidence justified that decision?"

These six stages form one continuous data path. Raw preservation protects the evidence; temporal alignment and normalization make observations comparable; the quality gate determines their suitability; event detection applies the domain logic; and the final record explains the result.

The value of this architecture comes from the boundaries between stages.

This is deliberately more than a sensor-fusion algorithm. It is a contract for how imperfect physical observations become software decisions.

The principle is straightforward: preserve what was measured, establish what it means, evaluate whether it is fit for use, and only then act on it.

Imagine a fleet operator whose mobile application scores driving behavior. Drivers receive alerts for harsh braking, and fleet managers use the events to identify potentially risky patterns.

One morning, a driver approaches a traffic light and brakes normally. The smartphone collects GPS-derived speed while the vehicle interface reports speed independently. The backend later records a harsh-braking event.

The driver disputes the alert. The vehicle did slow down, but not as abruptly as the application claims.

The engineering team examines the processing flow and discovers that the phone and vehicle streams were paired by arrival order. GPS updates were less frequent, and one observation represented an earlier point in the journey. During deceleration, the system compared that older speed estimate with a more recent vehicle measurement.

The discrepancy looked like physical behavior. Part of it was actually a timing problem.

The pipeline had accepted both values because they were syntactically valid. It had no mechanism to establish whether they were temporally comparable.

Figure 2. How a timing mismatch can create a misleading event (Source: created by the author)

The team introduces a temporal-alignment stage before event detection. Each observation retains its measurement timestamp, while arrival time is tracked separately. The pipeline evaluates the freshness of each observation and avoids comparing streams when timing uncertainty exceeds the application's defined tolerance.

The detector also stops treating every speed discrepancy as equivalent. When the measurements are not sufficiently aligned, it lowers confidence or abstains from generating a definitive event.

The team adds monitoring for timestamp offsets, stale observations, alignment failures, and event reclassification. These metrics help distinguish a change in driving behavior from a change in data quality.

This approach does not guarantee that every braking event will be classified correctly. It gives engineers a way to identify a measurement-comparison problem before treating it as driver behavior.

The same pattern applies to fleet diagnostics, trip reconstruction, usage-based insurance, and connected-vehicle analytics.

The lesson: before interpreting disagreement between sensors as physical behavior, establish whether the measurements are temporally comparable.

Time alignment does not solve the second major problem: orientation.

An accelerometer measures along the device's axes. A vehicle-relative interpretation assumes that the system knows how those axes relate to the vehicle. If the phone rotates, that relationship changes.

The gyroscope can help estimate rotation, and sensor-fusion algorithms can estimate orientation. Neither eliminates uncertainty automatically. Estimates may drift, the initial orientation may be unknown, and the phone can move independently of the vehicle.

A field named longitudinalAcceleration can therefore be misleading if it was calculated from device-relative measurements while the phone's orientation was uncertain.

The architecture should distinguish raw device-frame measurements from transformed estimates and preserve the assumptions behind each transformation.

Consider a mobile telematics application that detects cornering and sudden lateral movement using the phone's accelerometer and gyroscope.

A driver starts a journey with the phone secured in a horizontal dashboard mount. The application estimates orientation and interprets motion relative to the vehicle. Later, the mount loosens on a rough road, and the phone rotates. The driver continues straight.

The application detects apparent lateral movement and records an aggressive-turning event.

The sensor values changed, but the physical interpretation was wrong. The device's orientation changed, so the relationship between its axes and the vehicle's direction of travel was no longer the same.

This problem is easy to miss when testing only with a phone mounted in a fixed position. The algorithm may perform well in a controlled setup and fail when users reposition the phone, adjust the mount, or carry it during a trip.

Figure 3. The device frame is not automatically the vehicle frame (Source: created by the author)

The team makes orientation confidence an explicit input to event detection. Raw accelerometer and gyroscope observations are preserved, while transformed measurements carry metadata describing the estimated reference frame and the confidence in that transformation.

The detector no longer assumes that one phone orientation remains valid for the entire journey. It monitors orientation changes and identifies periods when the relationship between the device and vehicle is uncertain.

When orientation is reliable, the application can use transformed measurements according to its validated detection policy. When confidence falls, it can rely on other trustworthy evidence, reduce the confidence of the event, or abstain from making a definitive classification.

The team tests deliberate phone rotations, loose mounts, different mounting positions, and periods when orientation cannot be estimated reliably. It measures false positives and false negatives against a defined reference rather than assuming that a more sophisticated algorithm automatically improves accuracy.

This also improves the user experience. Instead of penalizing a driver for an uncertain observation, the application can indicate that it could not classify the event reliably.

The lesson: sensor accuracy and interpretation accuracy are different things. A sensor can report its measurement correctly while the application assigns that measurement the wrong physical meaning.

The same principle applies to phone-based activity recognition, wearable devices, robotics, and industrial IoT.

The quality gate is the fourth stage in the architecture, but its responsibility extends beyond checking whether sensor values look reasonable. It determines whether the available measurements are reliable enough for the specific decision an application intends to make.

The preceding stages preserve observations, establish temporal relationships, and normalize their measurement semantics. However, even after these steps, the resulting measurements may still contain uncertainty, missing samples, or inconsistencies. Without an explicit quality evaluation, individual event detectors must handle these conditions independently, often using different assumptions and fallback rules. This can lead to inconsistent decisions across the application.

I consider the quality gate a contract between the telemetry pipeline and the business logic that consumes its output. It makes the limitations of the available evidence explicit and defines what downstream components are permitted to do with it.

This section explores three aspects of that contract: why measurement quality must be evaluated in the context of the intended decision, how the system should distinguish between accepting, degrading, and abstaining from a result, and why abstention should be treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a processing failure.

Suppose a fleet application supports two functions: displaying the approximate route of a trip and identifying a short, aggressive braking maneuver.

The route display may tolerate a less frequent location update. The braking detector needs evidence that is sufficiently aligned in time and suitable for estimating a rapid change in speed.

Using the same universal threshold for both functions can be unnecessarily restrictive for one and dangerously permissive for the other.

Instead, each consumer should declare its requirements. The quality gate evaluates the observation against those requirements and communicates the outcome.

This approach also makes product trade-offs explicit. If a team wants more events at the expense of accepting weaker evidence, that decision becomes a documented policy choice that can be evaluated—not an accidental consequence of a permissive fallback in a detector.

Engineering teams often focus on maximizing the number of events detected. But a system that always returns an answer can create a false sense of certainty.

Abstention is useful when the evidence does not support the intended decision. It should not be treated as an exception that disappears into a log file.

The system should record why it abstained, whether additional data could resolve the uncertainty, and whether the decision needs to be revisited. For some use cases, waiting briefly for a delayed observation is reasonable. For others, the system may need to return an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome.

This is especially important when events influence human decisions, scores, or downstream automation. A clearly identified lack of evidence is often more useful than a precise-looking result that cannot be defended.

A quality-aware architecture is only as good as the team's ability to see it working. If the system records only the number of events generated, it becomes difficult to distinguish a genuine change in driving behavior from a change in sensor availability, application lifecycle, or processing logic.

I would monitor the quality pipeline alongside the business outcomes.

These measurements should be segmented where useful by device type, operating-system version, sensor source, application version, and collection conditions. Otherwise, a system-wide average may conceal a failure affecting a particular group of devices.

I would also connect quality metrics to event outcomes. If the number of harsh-braking events suddenly rises, the team should be able to investigate whether driving behavior changed, timestamp skew increased, or a new application version altered sampling behavior.

This requires a distinction between technical metrics and business metrics. Event counts and driver scores tell us what the application concluded. Freshness, alignment, and rejection metrics help explain whether the evidence behind those conclusions changed.

A smartphone sensor pipeline does not run in a perfectly controlled environment. Applications can move into the background, devices can enter power-saving modes, connectivity can disappear, and operating systems can constrain background execution.

The architecture should not assume that a requested sampling rate guarantees a continuous stream.

On the device, collection code should handle sensor unavailability, sampling gaps, lifecycle transitions, and local buffering. When connectivity returns, queued observations may arrive in a burst or out of order. The backend should therefore apply its temporal-alignment and duplicate-handling policies even when the data originated from a single phone.

The system should preserve the distinction between the time an observation was measured and the time it was uploaded. It should also make gaps visible rather than filling them silently with fabricated continuity.

These concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.

I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.

The goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.

A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.

The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.

The six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.

Freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.

Ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.

Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.

The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.

The phantom braking scenario shows why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.

The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

#9798. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

There is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

No. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Tips for vendors (plan 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.
