InfoQ Homepage Presentations From Fan-Out to Fast: Sub-100ms API Design in Distributed Systems

Saranya Vedagiri explains how to design resilient, low-latency distributed APIs under 100ms. Drawing on practical scale at eBay, she discusses hop-by-hop latency budgets, async fanout tradeoffs, thread pool sizing, caching, and circuit breakers. Learn actionable strategies to eliminate tail-latency bottlenecks and establish performance-first engineering practices.

Saranya Vedagiri is a Staff Engineer at eBay, where she designs and operates large-scale distributed systems with a focus on reliability and low-latency performance. Her work spans API design, service-to-service communication, caching strategies, and resilience patterns that keep critical flows fast under real production traffic.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Saranya Vedagiri: How many of you got the chance to take the Tube today? So many of you have taken the Tube. Have you ever wondered why is the line paused again, anytime in your experience when taking the Tube? I just see a couple of you leaning in. I would like to take the Tube design just like a system design in a distributed system. Just like how we have the map in our hand, it feels as if London is manageable. A couple of lines, a transverse, and you feel like everything is good. That's not the same when you take the actual journey. Your actual journey can have pauses and unexpected reason. That's not what you want. That's similar to a distributed system. When you look at the system diagram, it feels so comforting. A couple of boxes and arrows moving from one to another. You expect everything to go great.

That's not really what happens. When the downstream slows down, you have to retry. Then, when a cache miss happens, you again retry. You fall back to a database. All of this adds time. That is why latency is important. What we are going to do today is considering latency as a route plan. We are going to take each and every hop, make sure there is a budget assigned to each hop, and see how we can get the journey better and make sure one station is not acting as a bottleneck for your complete journey. Today, the title of our discussion is, "From Fanout to Fast: How Do We Build an API within sub-100 milliseconds in a Distributed Environment?" If you are a senior engineer, I will give you concrete patterns which you can go back and apply. If you are an architect, let's look at some of the tradeoffs and system constraints. If you are a leader, let's make sure you have enough information so you can prioritize what is right for the team.

I'm a staff engineer at eBay. I have nearly two decades of experience in the IT industry. Lately, most of my involvement is towards building low latency systems which are scalable and reliable. From my experience, one thing is very sure, building a low latency system is doable once, but if you have to keep it the way that it is always, then it needs a lot of engineering. That's where the real engineering is. Let's see how we can do that. This is why a repeatable process is important. We don't have any quick shortcuts to get it done.

Let's understand, what is the cost of a millisecond. When you compare 120 versus 80, it doesn't sound too dramatic. Users don't experience latency as numbers, they experience it as friction. Friction really compounds. What do we do about it? What we are going to do is we are going to see how we can take the complete request path and divide it into some components or parts and make sure we cap each part with a budget. We also know that when scale comes into picture, your latency drifts. Have you seen the scenario where the system that you are building, let's say you put up a cap limit of your latency to be like 30. This is in a normal scenario. When peak traffic hits, your graph suddenly bumps up to 60. When there is a dependency wobble, you see that the latency shoots up again to 120.

There's no steady graph, but there is always a bump here and there. What has changed? There is no change in your code. The code has remained the same throughout. What has actually changed is the frictions that happen, is the systems which are going down, is the retries which are happening, your thread contention, your queuing, all of these aspects have added to this. A better way to handle is to look at the complete request journey.

Here is what we will cover. We'll start off with assigning a budget to latency, and make sure every hop has its own budget. Then we'll take a look into a complete journey, and see all the things that could go wrong. We'll see a scenario and how that could be fixed. We'll move on to tradeoffs. Then, without measurement, there is no success. We don't know how far we are without measuring. We'll look at that. We'll look at what the future holds, and we'll wrap it up.

Latency budget. This is nothing but what your goal is versus what your system design is supporting. Let's say you want to build a recommendation engine which needs to respond within 50 milliseconds, because it's going to be used in multiple different components in your pages, exposed in emails and everything. How is your system design supporting this? That's what we need to see. How does it help, actually? When you have a concrete plan, it helps you with two things. One is prioritization. You don't really need to spend 100 milliseconds on a nice-to-have if you already know what is your cap limit. The other thing is alignment. It makes better alignment between the different teams. We don't need to explain each team between the product, the engineering, your quality teams about various aspects, because everybody comes to an alignment with one cause that they have to deliver things at a low latency.

Now what we will do is we will take the complete path from the client to the way that the client can receive the response and divide it into sub-parts, and make sure each part does not take more than what it is allocated. Here is a rough estimate of how we could break this down. There are a few things where we can utilize some buffer, but there are a few things which you cannot utilize a buffer. The edge layer, there's nothing we could do about it. Most of the content pull up your TLS, and the initial routing needs to happen here, which is going to take time, and you have to give it that. Let's cap it with 10 milliseconds. The next one comes the gateway. That's where your authentication and throttling happens, and you have to give it a 5 millisecond. Then next comes the application logic.

This is where it can be done in a single microservice or more. Just a pointer here. I think we have been overusing the terms of microservice where teams have started to really subdivide it into so many services that what could be done by one service is being done by four now. What we are forgetting is the network hop, which is involved in all of these things. We cap it at 30. Then the next one is the data access layer, where you definitely need an entity service, which is actually writing to your database, which could be whatever database that you're choosing. Then comes the buffer. It's better to save some buffer. Here we are adding 10 to 15 milliseconds as a buffer just to make sure there is enough time. Reality exists, so whenever there is a delay, you are just serving your buffer to make sure you have that time with you.

Next, we look at a sample journey, a request journey, and see how things can go wrong in this journey. This is simple, considering we already saw the budget allocation. Your request travels from the client to the edge, and then the authentication, then it moves to your application logic, your persistence layer, and the way back. Now some teams don't realize that there is a component for serialization when you send your response back. That is where the JSON payload translations happen. Sometimes they wonder, why is my application logic fast, but my API itself isn't? This is one reason. Having seen the path, where does the latency hide in all of these things? The network hop. When we take the network hop, we have the TLS handshake, the connection pools, we have DNS lookups, everything. What I would suggest is, if it's possible, removing one hop saves a lot of time than actually rewriting thousands of code.

If you think about this, so let's say we have an item service, which needs to call a couple of other services, like the item, detail service, which calls the seller details to fetch all the seller details. Then the feedback rating, the feedback reviews, the completed text of it, the image URL, everything. It has to call a number of downstream services. Now if each service takes a particular time, so now it is important to see whether we need to talk to all of these services synchronously or asynchronously, and how much of it is actually exposed to the outside clients. If it is an internal service, do we want to use gRPC? What that helps with, it helps with communication between two services, which could be faster if there is more data payload with sharing. If it is a REST service and if it is public-facing, then it makes sense to use JSON, because it's more meaningful when you read it.

The other thing is serialization. As I said, when your payloads are increasing, you have to pay for serialization. What can happen? For example, if I'm returning item details, I have a lot of information with me, title, description, SKU details, what is my last transaction, who bought my last item, so many information. Do I have to send all of this information for my client? My clients for an item service, could be search, could be cart, could be checkout, could be an email, could be some metrics. All of these clients, do all of them need the same information? Is there some customization which could be done based on who the client is? Do you need to use a REST service or do you want to use a GraphQL, because it is a read service. All of these discussions need to be done and decided. These are some things which could hide your latency.

Cold caches. What if there is a cache miss at the wrong moment? Then you have to fall back to the database, which adds up your latency. DB query shape. There are a few queries. Like, if you miss the tuning of the queries, if you miss the constraints, if the constraints are not built right, then it is going to take time, and you end up tuning it at the wrong moment after you are live. These are some things to be checked beforehand. Queuing and contention comes into play when we are using threads. If a downstream fails, the queue size increases, the thread contention increases. Now eventually you try to retry because you have not got the response. Your request comes pouring in. Now you have a lot of things to handle and the system eventually fails. Then the dependencies. When you have more dependencies, your total SLA is dependent on it, because that's from the slowest downstream that you are calling. Observability. If you're adding too much log, where is your tracing information? How much are you tracing? Are you doing 1%? Are you doing more than that? All these tiny pieces make a huge impact.

Now let's take a scenario and look at the fixes for it. Here is the case when we faced that. The p95 was looking fine, but the users still timed out. What happened was we got issues raised, from one of the clients, saying, I'm getting a lot of timeouts. When we look at our dashboard, our dashboard is green. We don't see pretty much. We don't really see that, because we are taking in billions of calls. For the client, they have millions of calls. Then even a small failure, in this case, it was less than 1% for us, but nearly 1% for them. If you take the example of the item service, if it's coming from the checkout, then every single transaction is valuable. Any single transaction, we don't want to result in a failure. That's exactly what we wanted to look at. How do we face this?

How do we investigate this problem? How do we solve this problem? When you're having your majority works, your p99 works, your p95 works, but that's where, in your p99, it's not the way that it has to. First of all, let's see how we went about investigating this. We need to take from the client how much logs they have. Try to map those into your system. Like, are you able to trace it out? This is why, if there are leaders in the group, it is important to make sure you have added all the observability metrics for your services, because there is no time after having an incident that you go back and add all of these things. Now, if you have not built dashboards for your p99, this is the time to build that. If you're having those dashboards, look at it. Now, what is the difference between a successful transaction and where it has timed out?

What is the bottleneck that you're seeing here? It could be some downstream is not returning, the cache lookup was a failure, we had to go back, retried so many times, it didn't work. What is that exact problem? Note down all those problems that you're seeing and compare it with the dashboards that you have. Does it correlate? Are you looking at your thread health? Are you looking at your queue size? Does it correlate somewhere? Are you looking at your DB dashboards. Did you receive peak load during that time? Did you look at the cache dashboards? Are you having cache misses? Are the cache calls increased? Look at all of that information which you have and see what corresponds. Now when you look at the cost, it's always tempting to say that it can be the retries that we did, or it is the cache request which has failed.

There can be so many causes which is not really evident at the first glance, and those could be retry amplification. I've seen some of the codes when reviewing. Every time there is a retry, they increase the retry timeout. First time it is 500, second time they add it to 1,000. What is the benefit of this? If you want to build a high latency system and you retry, you're capping it at 500 and 1,000, you're not in the game. Your service is already going to lose it. Make sure your retries make sense. If you're looking up from cache, if it is Redis Cache, usually it responds in 5 milliseconds. Do you want to cap it at 8 or 10, and then do a retry? Don't wait for 50 milliseconds and do a retry. Probability of you capping it lower and then doing a retry might result in a better one.

Maybe you are reaching a different pod. The other one would be thread pool starvation. Here, if an application is using just one thread pool for the entire journey, it has a good potential to bring the system down. We'll talk more in detail about thread pool in the coming slides. The next is database tail latency. There are situations where database is taking more time, maybe bad query, maybe you hit a wrong shard, hotspots, things like that. Observability gaps. You're logging too much of information. Then your GC or the JVM pauses. What do we do about it? In our case, we did three things, which actually helped us. The one is payload reduction. We were retaining a lot of information. Look at your maps. We had a key-value pair map, which was having user-related information. It had thousands of keys in it. We were returning this to 400-plus applications.

Not every application actually needs this. They probably need only 5 or 10 keys, but we were returning everything because that's all associated with the user. We didn't have the ability to request for a certain case. Now, once we changed that, that was helpful. Look at your response. Scan through each field one by one. Look to see if everything is making sense for the client, from the client perspective. Then, your retry discipline. Retry only if you're making idempotent calls. Here, again, you have to cap your limit and make sure you're giving thread pools separately for each of the downstream. That is what it is with thread pool guardrails.

I think now we started off with why a millisecond is important. We looked at budget. We also saw a request journey. How things could go wrong in that journey. Now it is time to look at some of the tradeoffs that are available. The first one is async fanout. We know what fanout is. Like one request turning into multiple. When we have such a fanout scenario, there are multiple options by which you can execute. One is doing things serially, the obvious way: one after the other. Or, see how much you could parallelize it in a couple of threads. Like whether you want to do two things at once. Then maybe your output needs to be fed for the other downstream calls. You take a judgment about it and do it. Then, if you're doing asynchronously, you also have options of running it in a separate background thread, or you want to drop an event.

Or let's say you make a fire and forget call. Like, what are the options that you have? What is making sense for your application at that moment? Maybe let's take an example to understand this better. If we take placing on an order as an example, when you take place order, there are a number of things which have to happen immediately, like after you hit on that place order button. One thing is you're supposed to receive your order confirmation email, the inventory has to get reduced. Your payment has to be made. You have to detect from the buyer, credit to the seller. Your metrics, you need to drop the metrics. Maybe giving this information to a couple of other downstream services which actually takes in this for the feedback and other things. Now when there are a lot of things, not all of these things have to happen serially.

When you take the item service response, where item has to call image, call seller details, call feedback and everything, again here there are a couple of things which needs to happen at the moment for sending the response back, but the couple of things need not happen synchronously. That is why we need to decide what needs to happen when, and see if you can move certain parts below the radar. When you want to do that asynchronously, making your configuration for a thread pool is very important. What is a thread pool? Let's compare it with, maybe you have a fixed number of workers in your kitchen. Let's say two workers. You have orders piling in. What happens? The two workers may not be able to do all the orders, and your orders are piling. Let's say you have very few orders, there's a very good chance that they bump onto each other.

Now, having this right configuration is very important. How could we go about it? What could help us to define what is the right configuration? This is where we need to check, what is our application doing? Is it an I/O intense work? Is it doing an I/O intense work, or is it doing a CPU intense work? Some examples could be, for CPU intense work, are you doing any algorithm processing? Are you doing image processing? Are you validating fields using your rules engine? Are you doing any encryption, decryption, or maybe tokenization? What are you actually doing? If you're doing all of these works, it is CPU intense work. Closer to your CPU cores, if you're using an 8-core system, maybe 8 threads, you should be good with this, with a normal load. Let's say if you're doing an I/O intense work, calling your REST service, calling your downstream, or waiting because you don't get the response, you have to wait.

You're looking at file. You're making a cache call, database call. All of these are I/O intense work. Since there is a waiting time involved, we need to make sure that you're adding more threads, taking this into account. A small example could be, if you are waiting for 80 milliseconds, and that particular downstream is capable of giving you a response in 20, the formula is the number of cores that you have times 1 plus 80 by 20, which nearly comes to about 40 threads. When you're having your CPU intense work, you are only at 8. If you're having an I/O intense work, you are at 40 now. Using the right number is very helpful. Your service could be doing both. Then you need to carefully check what your service is doing and make sure your limits are set based on that. This is no hard and fixed number.

It is more as a starting point where you should actually fine-tune it based on your results, based on the dashboards that you're seeing. Go back and fine-tune this. Also, there is one more important thing to understand, is, what is your incoming traffic? How much concurrent requests are you going to receive? That is also important to determine this thread count. A simple way could be from Little's Law, where, what is your latency? Latency into number of requests per second. If your latency is 50 milliseconds for your service and you are expected to get 500, then it's about 25 concurrent requests that you are seeing. This is even before the retries that you have to do, system getting abnormal, and things like that. This is just a starting number. Make sure you cap your threads at the right number. Along with the thread pool, the other thing which we need to be careful about is queuing.

Once you have set some number with your thread pool, if there are more requests, you need to make sure your queue size is also right, because that's where the next requests are going to be queued in. Now, let's say both your thread pool and your queue is full, then, what next? You need some rejection policy set up. What is your rejection policy? Have you carefully analyzed your rejection policy? Are you going to outright reject your request? Are you going to pick up any low priority work and remove that from your queue? What is that? You have to define that correctly, which will help you. Also, the other thing could be the memory, which you have to check, and things like that.

Next comes the caching. We don't expect everything to be returned by the service. You don't need to go to database to return every information through the service. There are moments that you have to leverage using cache. What type of a cache? What data do you put in your cache? What is the key that you're going to use in your cache? That's where all these engineering concepts lie. Are you going to use a single cache to look up all the information? Let's say, for the item information, do you want to add feedback into the cache? Is the review itself making sense or do you want to add the feedback score? Is adding item description making sense or do you want to add the price. What is making sense? What is the time? What is the benefit this is going to give? Of course, it's going to give you latency importance.

Because 5 milliseconds versus 30, and that's the tradeoff. Make sure you are building cache, which are multi-level, if possible. You don't want to make your cache bulky also. The payload in the cache shouldn't be bulky. You want to make sure that you are giving the right data, checking the payload size as well. Make sure it's not like more than a few KB. Using a cache is not going to solve all the problems until you have invalidation set right. If you're not invalidating your data as the data changes, if you're not making it accurate, then there is a chance that you're not showing the clients the right information. Then there is no point in using the cache. Invalidation becomes very important. How are you going to invalidate this data? There are a couple of options. If you set a fixed TTL, then till that time, the data is there and then it moves away.

Is that the practical approach that you want to take? Sometimes you want to change it when the actual data is being changed by the user. Then you want an event-based approach. You also have like version-based. Choose version-based only if you are sure about, is there a reliable plan to choose the exact version because you don't want to get into trouble of choosing what is the right version to be picked up. There is also another concept of stale-while-revalidate. This is where you know the information is stale, but it's ok to return that. You have to determine who are your clients. You don't want to have a checkout reading price from a cache. You want the most accurate information. You need to go to the DB for it. Choose what is your application doing, the responsibility of the application. How much delay is your client acceptable? That could be different between different clients.

If you're sending an email, it's fine to build something which is not really accurate, which can be eventually consistent. That is fine. Choose based on your clients as well. Then, we also have the option of using group-based, where it is best advised for derived or aggregated views. A general rule of thumb, maybe if you're experimenting it for the first time, will be start it with a TTL and then fine-tune it. Once you fine-tune it, use the event-based approach.

You know that you want to cache. You know how you can have the right data. Now you need to understand that data classification is important. You don't want to get into any of those compliance issues where you have added the wrong data, especially when you're in the financial industry. What are the data classifications available? Public data, anything which is public. When you search for an item, you get all this listing information. You get seller details, like what is the seller's name? Where is he selling this item from? These details. These are all publicly available. It's ok to cache it. What about internal data? Some of those unique IDs. You have UUID. Do you want to expose it outside? What about your item ID? Do you want to expose it outside? These are things that need to be determined. This is something that you need to work with your InfoSec team to understand what is the organization's level of classification, and how much they want to expose it, add it to a cache, and things like that.

What about confidential data, like name, address, phone number, things like this? Definitely, we need to encrypt it or tokenize it. Whatever is the best fit or recommendation from the InfoSec team. Now this is a time where we need to think, does it make sense to add it in cache? We are going to cache because we want to reduce the time. Now if you're adding a confidential data in the cache, be mindful that you need to pay for decrypting it or de-tokenizing it. Are you ready to accept that? Is your system ok to do that? Then, about classified information. Your SSN number, your passport number, all of this information, a strict no. You cannot cache this data.

Next, we'll move on to circuit breakers. Circuit breakers are very helpful. It helps you contain your problem area to a specific region. It doesn't allow the entire system to be brought down. Instead, it contains the problem in one specific area. In that way, circuit breaker is very important. If you take a mental model. What happens, let's say when a downstream fails, and you have 10 downstream calling, and one of the downstream suddenly starts failing, the queue starts to build up, your thread pool queue is also high, your backup queue is also high. Now, as per your system logic, you try to retry and you also have incoming requests. There is a complete possibility of system being down. You are actually having a self-inflicted failure. Even if there is a request which does not need this downstream A, the request could fail for them. A circuit breaker helps in that.

It helps you contain that. It is important to use this. When the circuit breaker is open, it's not going to allow any request. It's going to allow time for the particular downstream to prepare itself, to come back up. When it partially opens up to send a few requests is to see whether it succeeds. Once it succeeds, it sends the remaining requests. This is very helpful.

Then, what about fallbacks? Maybe we could take this example. When you're viewing an item on a search, you actually see this hottest item trigger, or you see this, five people are viewing onto this item. I have 10 purchased this item two hours back, or an hour back. All of these are hot information which are available. You need to be more accurate to give this information, or maybe nearly accurate. What if we don't have this? What if the service which returns this information are failing? Then you probably go and use your fallback text, which is like, maybe, yes, this is a hot item. Many people are viewing. We had more transactions. Don't give the exact number. This is the use of fallback. Consciously decide based on what your service is doing. Check if there are any places where you could use this tactic of a fallback.

It doesn't have to be a static text. It could also be defaulting to certain numbers based on the situation. The other one is data partitioning, which is mostly underrated. The main theme is to avoid hotspots. Why do we want to avoid hotspots? Because we want to distribute the traffic to all the shards possible. When you're deciding about partitions, make sure you choose a key which will give you a unique distribution across. Don't choose something like, I'm going to put all my hot sellers into one shard, like the top sellers into one shard. When there is a specific season, for example, Thanksgiving in the U.S., it's going to make all the requests go into that shard. It does not make sense to divide your sharding based on this theme. Rather use a key which is very generic: maybe the ID of the user itself, maybe his login name.

Use things which are generic, and make sure that gives a default distribution or a common distribution into all the shards. Sometimes due to regulations, it is also required that you need to split your data based on the region. Like EU region, you need to have a separate shard. U.S. region, you need to have a separate shard. This does not solve the problem because, again, if you have a seasonal event, it's going to go into that particular shard. That is why it is important to subdivide it based on the other keys that you have.

Now that we have seen a quick recap, we started with why is latency important, why is being fast important. We saw a request journey. We saw a list of tradeoffs. Now, until we measure, we don't know how good we are performing. That is why measuring things is really important. A measure could tell you how long things went well, or did not go well. Tracing will tell you why something happened. If you're not having tracing, you are missing out on something, on identifying why the problem even happened. Tracing is very important. If you haven't built it, it's time to actually build this. There could be themes, with the teams coming up saying, "My Redis is failing. My DB looks fine, but my cache calls are failing." How are we figuring out all of these things? Only because we have tracing built. You are able to take just the unique ID, look through the complete request, and see where exactly the problem has happened.

If you are able to identify, that's because you have tracing built in. Let's move on to having SLOs. Before maybe going into SLOs, I want to touch base on SLIs, service level indicators. They are like direct metric information. Let's say you are getting 100k requests per second. Then let's say around 95k requests have succeeded, and the remaining 5k were not successful. This 95% is your success rate, or your application's availability is just 95%. The same thing, you could track for your error rates, you could track for a specific error also. You have that specific downstream, you can tie it based on the feedback system, what is the availability of the feedback system. All of those things could be done. You could also have measures like, how many of my requests is responding well within 200 milliseconds? If the number was 99.8, then that is the time that you have done it.

How do we tie this to a goal? That's where SLO comes in, service level objective. Let's say you want to make sure in a 30-day period, I want the availability of my system to be 99.9. Then that is your SLO. What happens when you set this up? You are going to be alerted. The team is going to be alerted. The leaders are going to know, when an SLO, the buffer, the time that you had, if you're utilizing that buffer in a week, which you had set for a month, then it is time to pause on all your velocity works that you're doing, and first fix the system. Did I make a wrong judgment about the SLO? My SLO number itself, did I do a mistake in configuring that, or should I go back and check my application service? Check the path, where is it going wrong?

Has it been happening consistently? Then there is something to do about it. Then there is some refactoring which needs to be done. There is no one solution which can fix it. You have to do small things at every journey to make sure that you're getting it right. This is where SLO is very helpful. Thread pool observability. We saw about thread pools and the importance of thread pool. Now, if we don't have an observability dashboard, you are not going to know whether your queue is getting built up. Am I getting an alert for it? Setting up alerts, before that, you need a dashboard. We need dashboards for active threads. What is my queue size? What is a completed task count? Then, what is my rejection rate? If I have information for all of these, then it's helpful for me to fine-tune during the next iteration.

Now that we have seen about how we could measure, how we could fix it, we have seen a lot about technical things going wrong, technical aspects going wrong. Now it is time to look at the human side of things. What is within our control? What can we do as a team to get this done? That's where culture comes into picture. During planning, are we talking about SLA? Are we talking about latency? Are we talking about what is our goal? During retrospective, did we talk about the last incident which happened? What was the last issue where you had to come back online and check things on a weekend? Did you have to spend your night over it? What was that incident? Are we discussing it as a team? Are we trying to fix our dashboards? Are we trying to fix our alerts? I know that teams set up alerts only in Slack, and your Slack thread is filled up with all these alert messages, nobody is looking into it.

Are we looking into that? These are things collectively which a team needs to take up, like during your planning session, during your retrospective. This is nothing but performance and review. What are some of the anti-patterns which we need to avoid? Considering staging data. Let's say you're doing a load test in staging and taking that number for your production. That's no way the same. Your environment in your lower region is not the same as what you're doing in production. Do not take that as a benchmark. If you're going live, maybe start with 1%, 2% traffic. Or even better, start it with traffic mirroring, if that is allowed. You mirror your traffic and see whether your new flow that you've added is performing at the same level as earlier in production. Is it delaying your latency? Is there something that you need to restructure? The other things could be synchronous logging, where you're logging too much information.

What is the future holding for us? There are a lot of things, like capabilities around adaptive routing where routing could be done to regions which are having less traffic. AI-assisted predictions, you can have models to predict, this is the hot cache. Make sure you can warm it up beforehand. You can use predictive warming. Edge-native executions, all of these are in the future.

Let me give you some information which you could try before the weekend. When you go back, what could you do? Choose a simple flow in your application, from end to end. Note it down. Work with your lead. Is there any journey that could be removed? Is there any duplicate logic? I've also seen these patterns when I'm reviewing code between the teams. If there is a dependency X, and you have three flows, like A is calling B, B is calling C. You always have this X which is getting called in all the flows. You tend to have that one service which everybody wants. What do we go about it? Is there anything that you can do about changing it? These are all things that you can check. Now, instrument it, and budget. You'll note down what is the graph. If you don't have a p99 dashboard, create one.

Note down what was the current latency. If it is at 500, yes, note it down. Look at the different junctions, your paths. Note down what each path has taken up. Now, where do you want to go from here? What is your budget? Cap it. Make improvements. Remove that unnecessary call. Rephrase it. Add thread pools. Parallelize it, if it's possible. Add cache if it's not there. Do all of these things, and take a result out of it. Run an L&P and take a result out of it. Now you can check the before and after metrics. I would like to leave with one quote. We are what we repeatedly do, so excellence is not an act, but a habit. I hope we inculcate that as a habit.

Participant 1: With regards to p95 and p99, what are they? Is it percentile?

Participant 2: I have one question around serialization and that you mentioned that we should clear up if it is not required. How do we measure the cost between clearing up the data before it gets serialized and to be returned versus just sending the entire data and then hoping that it will work?

Saranya Vedagiri: This is where your logging is helpful. Let's say you're calling x downstream service and you have the log from your application level and you also have the logging from your downstream. They will tell you, I received the request at 10, I returned back at 10, 10, or whatever, that milliseconds. In your logging, you would have not got the time that they had mentioned, so look at that. There is a buffer in between. Is that adding up, between what they say as they have sent to what you have received? There can be only a certain buffer for your network. If you are seeing a 50 milliseconds difference, then there is something going wrong. Is it your queue or is it your size? There is no one direct indicator, but it could be either of these two things.

#9790. Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

New agentic AI solution leverages APIs to collect compliance evidence from systems and applies it to over 30 frameworks with no duplicate work.

SEATTLE, November 18, 2026 — Strike Graph, the enterprise AI-native governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) management platform, today announced a new integration solution that seamlessly connects to any software API to automatically collect compliance evidence from it. With Integration AI, organizations using the Strike Graph platform are no longer limited to a fixed integration catalog. They simply indicate the system they are using and Strike Graph builds a native integration that pulls compliance evidence from it automatically.

Once connected via an API, the Strike Graph platform employs an AI research agent to read the vendor’s public API documentation and draft a build specification. Concurrently, a second AI agent builds the complete integration across Strike Graph’s backend, user interface, and evidence pipeline. Integrations connect API-to-API, and customers never install agents or software inside their own infrastructure, which is critical for maintaining enterprise-grade security.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

“For compliance to be successful, access to evidence must be quick, easy, and continuous, but integration with existing tools often presents a challenge,” said Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. “Integration AI has empowered Strike Graph to overcome those roadblocks and accomplish all three of those requirements at once. If it has an API, Strike Graph can collect evidence from it. Furthermore, since Strike Graph’s evidence model is graph-based, evidence from a newly built integration automatically counts toward every framework a customer pursues, including SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, with no duplicate work.”

As with all Strike Graph evidence collection integrations, Integration AI builds secure integrations that are restricted to read-only operations by default. Each one carries an endpoint allowlist that ratifies against the vendor’s real API documentation, which guarantees evidence collection can observe a customer’s systems but never change or impact them.

Strike Graph keeps strict separation where credentials are never touched by Integration AI.The build process works outside of the core governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) program itself, building the connection with no access to any customer secrets. Credentials and other sensitive data live in a securely managed secrets vault, and the build spec is scanned and automatically rejected if any credentials are detected in it.

With Integration AI, vendor documentation is treated strictly as data and never as instructions, which blocks prompt-injection attempts hidden in third-party content. The AI build environment holds no publishing rights, and a separate locked-down step does the publishing.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

Builds sit behind an approver allowlist and a kill switch, and humans are always in the loop to review the research plan before build starts, after code has been written, and before anything is deployed to production. The AI can only propose changes, not ship them, and every integration requires a human engineering review.

Once built, Integration AI runs evidence scripts in self-contained isolated sandbox environments with no shared code paths, so a flaw in one integration can’t spread to another.

Integration AI is available to Strike Graph customers today. For more information, visit www.strikegraph.com.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

#9789. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9788. Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

The state-sponsored threat group is using data stolen from one victim to target others via convincing impersonations and social engineering attacks.

The Russian cyber-espionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships.

It's a tactic that researchers at Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) observed the attacker deploy with clinical efficiency in two separate compromises involving US organizations over the past year.

In the first intrusion, late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic actors later used that material to impersonate an employee of the first organization for a successful social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization.

The activity, GTIG researchers said, shows how traditional social engineering is becoming more closely tied to attacks on cloud identities. Once inside an organization's cloud environment, an attacker can gather the kind of internal information that makes a message from a supposedly trusted colleague or business contact much harder to spot as a scam.

Related:Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," GTIG researchers wrote in a blog post. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Cold Relic (also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) is a cyber-espionage group that Google researchers have been tracking — and disrupting — since 2015. The US government has assessed the outfit as working within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) and tasked with collecting information of political and strategic interest to Moscow.

Though low-profile, Cold Relic has notched up numerous high-value targets including defense contractors, government officials, and NGOs across North America and Europe. One of its favorite post-compromise activities, according to GTIG, is to steal emails and data that can help it establish "authentic pretexts" and convincing impersonations when reaching out to other potential targets.

In the first intrusion in late 2025, Cold Relic used stolen credentials for a super admin account to access a US organization's cloud environment. The attackers routed their activity through a residential proxy located near the organization, so their connections appeared to originate from a familiar geographic area. The attacker repeatedly kept sending the actual account holder multifactor authentication (MFA) push notifications until the overwhelmed user approved one.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

After gaining access, Cold Relic actors registered their own device on the network and established additional ways to authenticate to it, including via passkeys, backup MFA codes, and additional rogue MFA devices. The threat group used the stolen Super Admin user privileges to exfiltrate the organization's cloud storage, including full employee lists, email conversations, and organizational directories and contact lists. The threat actors then initiated several anti-forensics measures that allowed it to maintain access to the compromised network for several months.

In the second attack, earlier this year, Cold Relic impersonated an employee of the first company to contact an individual at a second organization through an encrypted messaging app. The threat actors sent the unsuspecting target phishing links disguised as documents relevant to their ongoing conversation.

After stealing the victim's Microsoft Entra ID credentials and authentication tokens, Cold Relic used them to access the organization's Google Workspace environment through its federated single sign-on system. The attackers then helped themselves to files from the compromised user's cloud drive while also seeking out email archives, chat records, credentials, personnel information, and other data of potential intelligence value.

Related:AI Agents Zip From Flaw Discovery to Root Access in 11 Minutes

"Cold Relic is highly adept at leveraging social networks and impersonation of key individuals to achieve a realistic pretense for reaching out to the targeted individual or organization," Wes Shields, security engineer at GTIG, tells Dark Reading. "Once they have achieved their initial access goal, they move quickly to maintain persistence and exfiltrate data."

The lesson for organizations is to train employees to be wary of unexpected messages, particularly when they arrive through communication channels a supposed colleague or business contact doesn't normally use. If a message seems unusual, employees should verify the sender's identity through a separate, previously established channel before responding or acting on it, Shields advises.

"In today's hyper-connected world, it is impossible to have employees not be reachable via multiple channels, and attackers are taking advantage of this," he says.

Joseph Spero, principal incident response consultant at Google, recommends other measures to limit the damage from identity-based attacks. These include enforcing phishing-resistant MFA, restricting and auditing passkey registrations, hardening MFA registration procedures, and auditing OAuth grants.

"Short-lived sessions and the principle of least privilege will limit the potential scope of access when credentials are compromised," he says. "When a compromise is suspected, mandate session revocation in addition to resetting passwords and MFA mechanisms."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9787. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9786. Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Nigeria faced more than double the cyber threats of the previous year, with Angola and Kenya also in the top 5 most-attacked countries globally.

Organizations in Africa faced an average of 3,834 cyberattacks per week in October, a jump of 38% from a year earlier, making the continent the most-attacked region for the first time in more than a year.

Nigeria, Angola, and Kenya were among the top-five most targeted countries, with Nigeria topping the list with nearly 6,700 attacks targeting organizations in the country every week; that marks a 140% increase over October 2025, according to data published by Check Point Research earlier this month. The nations are among those rapidly pushing technological transformation of their infrastructure, expanding connectivity, investing in digital services, and putting sensitive data in network-connected applications and storage.

The fast transformation is exposing more opportunities for attackers, says Shayimamba Conco, chief technology officer and security evangelist in the Office of the CTO at Check Point Software.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"All this rapid digital expansion is now happening within the region, but then, at the same time, this [expansion] is outpacing improvements in security maturity," he says, adding that security improvements are uneven across the continent. "Yes, some areas — let's say for example, South Africa — it's adopting cybersecurity at a much quicker rate than the rest of the Africa region, but there will be those regions which are still lagging behind a bit."

The significant increase in average weekly attacks pushed African organizations past those in Latin America as the favored targets of cyberattackers. In the first quarter of 2026, Latin America averaged more than 3,000 attacks per week, surpassing the approximate 2,700 attacks targeting African organizations. In September, the two regions essentially tied in terms of attacks, with Africa once again becoming the most popular target in October.

Globally, organizations experienced an average of 2,550 weekly cyberattacks in October, down 9% from September but up a third from the previous year. While Africa encountered the most weekly attacks, both Latin America and Asia-Pacific regions saw a greater-than-average number — 3,483 and 3,436, respectively.

Globally, cyberattacks focused heavily on the education sector, with the average academic institution suffering more than 5,900 attacks per week, up a third from the same month in 2025. The education sector has topped the global list of popular targets every month, with organizations made attractive to attackers because of their large data sets and reliance on legacy systems, says Conco.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"There is a lack of budget when it comes to not just IT, but specifically cybersecurity," he says. "A junior IT engineer has to manage these vast environments, which are hard to lock down by nature, because you've got all these students who need access to all these applications and resources."

In Africa, however, cyberattackers most often targeted financial services, government agencies, and the energy sector, according to Check Point's data.

The countries are racing to improve their cybersecurity postures and address persistent threats. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) continues to work on the details of the nation's cybersecurity and cloud-sovereignty policies. Last month, Operation Serengeti 3.0 — a joint task force between Interpol and 20 African countries — led to the arrest of more than 1,500 suspects and the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds. In August, Operation Jackal IV targeted West African crime syndicates, leading to more than 200 arrests.

Check Point also flagged the use of AI in companies as a potential weak point, finding that about 2.9% of prompts to generative AI and large language models (LLMs) posed a high risk of leaking sensitive information. The risk is steadily increasing over time, from 2.3% in August to 2.5% in September.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Interpol has also observed that attackers are increasingly using AI in a way that has impacted African nations. In its African Cybercrime Assessment Report 2026, Interpol found that 55% of reported cybercrimes across Africa used AI to some degree.

"Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region," Neal Jetton, Director of Interpol’s Cybercrime unit, said in a statement in August. "AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. However, we see that when countries work together, cybercriminal infrastructure can be identified, disrupted and dismantled."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9783. Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Bot-driven fraud and holiday social engineering attacks stretch across many weeks, straining security teams and small businesses alike.

Cyber experts have long drawn connections between the accelerated volumes of holiday shopping and threat actors looking for opportunities to take advantage, but as the festive season kicks off, it's important to remember that security posture during this time period is a marathon — not a sprint.

Verizon today published survey results for its holiday trends report, tracking the insights of 600 small business owners and decision-makers in the US. Of those surveyed, 11% said they have dealt with a cyberattack or data-security incident during the holidays, and a third expect to increase cybersecurity investments this holiday season compared with last year.

Meanwhile, managed security services firm VikingCloud this week published a report surveying security and IT leaders which made even steeper claims: a full 86% of respondents said their business has faced at least one successful cyberattack in the past 12 months, and a whopping 98% said at least one came during the 2025 holiday season. And the Retail & Hospitality Information Sharing and Analysis Center (RH-ISAC) last year said the holiday season continues to be the most active fraud environment from a defender standpoint.

Related:Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Some reasons behind the prominence of cyberattacks during this time period are straightforward: Many cybersecurity teams experience lighter staffing during holiday periods and weekends (leaving the door open for easier ransomware attacks). The chaos of the holiday season also means online services and retailers are inundated with activity, giving threat actors cover. And on the social engineering front, the holidays give plenty of pretext for threat actors conducting phishing campaigns (fake emails promising unbelievable Black Friday deals, charity scams, and so on).

Some teams may take this as a cue to prepare for a few select days or weeks of this last part of the year, such as Black Friday or the week leading up to Christmas. But new research around one narrow corner of the threat landscape suggests that may not be wise.

One of the less-discussed types of threat activity retailers face each season is an influx of malicious bots.

F5 today published a study dedicated to automated threat activity leading up to Black Friday. The report analyzed bot and automation traffic across three Black Friday shopping seasons (2023 to 2025) using data from F5 Distributed Cloud Bot Defense. It covers retailers in three retail sub-industries: fashion, e-commerce, and quick-service restaurants (QSR). The report's authors observed that overall automation rose across the three seasons, from 17.4% of transactions in 2023 to 18.5% in 2024, and then 28.6% in 2025.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

The types of activity differ across industries, but F5 observed bots being used for product scraping and inventory hoarding, credential stuffing and account takeover, fake account creation (to claim new user offers), and gift card cracking (inserting gift card numbers into balance checkers to test for valid accounts).

In terms of trends overall, cyberattackers are increasingly leaning toward Web stores over mobile APIs, and a broad rise in bot sophistication over time. But one of the most notable conclusions that F5 researchers made is that there's no single best date to defend. Attackers start their bot onslaught weeks before Black Friday, and continue it well into the weeks after.

As Sean Murphy, F5's field chief information security officer (CISO) for North America, tells Dark Reading, "The data shows that automated activity can be elevated well before the shopping weekend, and the busiest day for automation varied dramatically from year to year."

Bot traffic does not necessarily reflect all threat activity, but there may be a broader lesson here: that steeling your security hygiene for the holiday season is not a few single days or weekends to prepare for but a broader stretch of time that spans from early November to the end of the year. Murphy says security teams "should have monitoring and protections in place throughout the shopping season rather than scaling them up only for Thanksgiving week."

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

For those in ecommerce dealing with Web and mobile APIs, he urges ensuring protection isn't substantially weaker on one than the other.

"Web traffic had much higher automation rates among the retailers studied, but the report specifically cautions against interpreting that as evidence that APIs are inherently safer. Where API protection is weaker, attackers can shift toward that channel," he says. "And because the dataset contains both simple scripts and automation designed to imitate legitimate users, defenses need to account for a spectrum of bot sophistication rather than relying on a single detection technique."

Finally, he recommends organizations prioritize targeted employee security awareness and training, particularly for those teams handling customer accounts, payments, and other sensitive information. "Many attacks still begin with social engineering and credential theft, so employees need to know how to recognize suspicious requests and protect account access."

Chris Flood, senior vice president and CRO of Verizon Business, tells Dark Reading that small businesses can reduce their risk with four fairly simple steps: require multifactor authentication, train employees how to spot scams, keep guest Wi-Fi separate from payment systems, and keep software and devices updated.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

#9782. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.
