#9733. Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Ransomware isn't slowing down. A new framework gives security teams the edge to trace attackers back to their source.

It's a now-familiar scenario: "Warning" abruptly displays on the computer screen as the system locks down. A ransom note follows, threatening data extortion and continued disruptions if a demand is not met. Although it may seem sudden at the moment, the attack was actually the final step in what may have been years of planning, all carried out by a sprawling, interconnected network of underground actors.

But a new framework based on an identity graph analysis, developed by Flare threat researcher Assaf Morag, aims to help defenders and law enforcement take a more proactive approach to ransomware risk by better understanding who they're up against. When applied during research, the framework can uncover the inner workings of these operations, including indicators of compromise (IoCs) that are critical to incident-response investigations. Researchers can also use it to find connections among various threat actors and groups, which is increasingly important as new groups emerge each year.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

Mapping and understanding the connections among the various ransomware gangs is also vital when it comes to documenting the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that ransomware groups use against organizations daily. Threat actors are highly adaptable, developing, buying, or renting new tools all the time to bypass endpoint detection and response (EDR) and to craft more convincing phishing emails. So the more available data about their operations, the more predictable their behaviors become for defenders.

Morag plans to debut his repeatable investigative methodology for mapping criminal organizations in a briefing at Black Hat Europe 2026. He will walk through the framework step by step; anyone can use it to reproduce the research or apply the same process to a new investigation.

Building a framework wasn't Morag's original goal. He first set out to study how initial access brokers (IABs) operate on Dark Web forums. But he realized the interconnected web of threat actors was too vast to dissect using available resources. His efforts to connect gang operators and affiliates to IABs actually took two long months of manual work, which wasn't a useful process for such a swiftly moving threat landscape. That's when Morag decided to develop a framework to help graph the activity. Once it was ready, the same research took only three hours.

To build the framework, Morag went into detective mode, gathering clues from forums and chat posts and sorting them into various buckets for "hard evidence" versus "soft evidence." The first included factors like specific messaging IDs, emails, or chat handles, while writing styles, typos, and reused phrases fell into the latter. Once he was able to verify a clue, he could use it to search for other connections. Eventually, the confirmations expanded into a massive map of connected identities with 21 personae, active over 17 years, with 5,437 posts.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Morag's findings support how ransomware attacks are rarely conducted by a single group from start to finish, and how operations often mirror legitimate businesses with everyone playing their role. That makes it hard to parse out exactly who's who.

That became obvious when Morag came across a notification posted to a Dark Web forum, translated from Russian, that read, "We are the oldest international Russian ransomware affiliate program." The group claimed to be a private program that emerged in 2018. But based on underground forum discussions, he noticed that some members had been active since 2010.

Tracking Tox IDs was the primary way Morag traced the connections, unveiling the true identity behind the fake personae and generic aliases threat actors use, like "John" or "Michael." Ransomware ecosystems commonly use communication platforms like Tox, Discord, Telegram, and Jabber to conduct payment negotiations with organizations or to recruit new affiliates, among other actions.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

When communicating with someone through a specific Tox address, Morag knew he was reaching one consistent endpoint, whether cloud-based or someone's personal computer. Either way, it's the same device every time, which matters because threat actors often operate under multiple aliases.

"He can change his name, but if I can take these identifiers and connect them together, that could be a way to look beyond the persona's name, which is usually fake, and that's exactly what I did," Morag tells Dark Reading.

During the course of investigation, Morag discovered six layers of operational roles across the business flow:

The homemade ransom layer: Useful for defenders to study, these are the people who develop ransomware strains, loader malware that bypasses antivirus and EDR, and infostealer payloads.

The ransom deployment layer: The gang operators and their affiliates who select the ransomware/malware, deploy it, and extort the victims.

Pen-testers: Folks who probe for weaknesses to find ways into organizations.

The dealers: IABs that buy and sell that initial access, like a sales department for cybercrime. (Morag was able to pinpoint seven individuals active for over nine years, spanning 50 forums and a whopping 1,300 events.)

Fraud recovery: Organizations that perform diagnostics, negotiate with attackers, and arrange settlements with victims.

Crypto draining: Those that process stolen seed phrases and private keys at scale and cross-sell crypto services to ransomware victims to compromise and drain wallets.

While piecing it together, one link particularly surprised Morag: a tie between supposed good-guy fraud-recovery firms and the ransomware deployers. Companies claim to help ransomware victims but secretly defraud them, he notes, and victim organizations have no clue.

Up until the fraud recovery layer in the business flow, everything was done in Russian. After that, Morag noticed an intentional switch to the English language. Once the ransomware locked an organization's system down, the ransomware deployers swooped in, posing as legitimate businesses looking to provide recovery services. They installed tools on victims' systems, ran diagnostics, offered data recovery, and legal compliance services, Morag says.

"This is not new, and we've also seen a few cases in the past month in the US. These kinds of organizations that help other organizations fight against ransomware were actually defrauding them," Morag explains. "I haven't seen anyone make the connection between those who do the recovery fraud and those that actually deploy the ransom, which is really amazing."

While deep in the underground forums, it also became clear to Morag how much threat actors value their reputations. For instance, on Exploit, "a reputable Russian market" where attackers pay $100 to $150 and undergo a test to get in, Morag observed infighting as threat actors accused one another of not being legitimate. The forum is a place where "you don’t want to lose your reputation" or your access, he stresses, because it's where threat actors discuss sensitive dealings, such as zero-day and known vulnerability exploits, and forge new ransomware-as-a-service partnerships. Looking into these disputes offered critical intelligence about how operations run because threat actors will throw each other under the bus by revealing what tools they use, how they move money, or what access they are trading.

Exploit, Morag says, is "a real gold mine because it explains how they work, what they're doing, the level of leadership, and who reports to who."

Exploit was one of more than 40 underground forums he visited that, when analyzed together with the framework, revealed the inner workings of cybercrime gangs. Unmasking the players provides more evidence for organizations to fight back against ransomware as the threat disrupts everything, from Coca-Cola production to Japanese frozen food.

The framework can't directly help organizations push back against ransomware, but it does provide much-needed contextual data for the private and public sectors as problems persist. Morag is applying the framework to help with attacks against financial systems — an obviously huge target for threat actors — for example. He also applied it to investigate another ransomware group more recently and says it yielded helpful results.

Real insight into a large operation like the one Morag discovered, knowing it included a fake fraud recovery layer, may also make organizations think twice about negotiating. They never know who's on the other line.

"It's [about] knowing your enemy," Morag says.

#9732. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9731. US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Trump named Kirsten Davies as Acting National Cyber Director, bringing greater industry experience to the role amid recent outages and rising geopolitical tensions.

The Office of the National Cyber Director will have a new, more technically experienced director at the helm, but how that might impact US cyber policy remains to be seen.

President Donald Trump on Nov. 19 tapped Kirsten Davies to lead the White House Office of the National Cyber Director, replacing Sean Cairncross, who is leaving the administration. Last December, Davies was appointed the chief information officer of the Department of Defense.

In a Nov. 20 news release, the White House said Davies "will drive an America First cyber strategy that treats cybersecurity as national security and keeps the United States dominant and secure in cyberspace." Upon last Thursday's announcement, Davies became Acting United States National Cyber Director, though she requires Senate confirmation to gain permanent directorship.

In a post on social media platform X, Davies wrote that the US has an opportunity "to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."

Related:Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Though not officially tied to Davies' appointment, Cairncross's departure occurred amid a number of outages affecting the public sector. Just this month, there was the outage against the Federal Aviation Administration that lasted for days, as well as an NSA communications network outage that apparently resulted from a software update. Other disruptions hit major banks and Microsoft services.

Melinda Marks, senior research director and chief analyst of cybersecurity at Omdia (an Informa TechTarget property), tells Dark Reading the outages seen in recent weeks have created significant speculation about US security posture. As such, Davies's appointment comes at a time when cybersecurity's role in national security is "more important than ever."

A source close to the White House told Dark Reading sister publication Cybersecurity Dive that Trump fired Cairncross over concerns regarding his cybersecurity credentials; a source told Semafor's Ashley Gold Cairncross resigned of his own volition.

Jacob Krell, senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that Cairncross is primarily an election lawyer who admitted at his June 2025 confirmation hearing that he had no technical background in cyber. Meanwhile, Davies has previously held security leadership roles at Unilever, The Estée Lauder Companies, Barclays, Hewlett-Packard, and Siemens.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

"It is a definite shift from a political appointee to one with much more experience in the industry," he says. "Given the string of massive outages and rising geopolitical tensions, it could not come at a better time."

It remains to be seen how a new National Cyber Director appointment may shape the future of cybersecurity in the US; should she be appointed, Davies stands to have substantial influence, given she would serve as Trump's primary adviser regarding cybersecurity policy and strategy.

Since Trump began his second term at the beginning of 2025, the makeup of US cyber has shifted immensely, with a culling of public sector cyber personnel, a lean into AI technologies, the shuttering of the Cyber Safety Review Board, and more.

Krell says he expects Davies's appointment to potentially shift cyber funding from AI-as-opportunity toward capacity-related expenditures, such as people, test environments, and change control. And as global tensions rise, he expects to see more focus on infrastructure and industrial control systems (ICS).

"Last week showed what machine-speed patching does to human-sized teams," he argues. "AI gets reclassified in the process, from capability accelerator to governed risk."

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

#9730. AI Could Become the Front Door to Digital Banking

Over the last several years, we have witnessed a real boom in AI technologies. Companies have been experimenting with agents, launching AI assistants, and trying to integrate new capabilities into existing products.

However, the initial enthusiasm is gradually colliding with reality. Building an impressive demo is much easier than launching a safe, secure, and reliable product for millions of users.

This is particularly evident in the banking sector, where companies work with sensitive financial data, face strict regulatory requirements, and where the cost of any mistake can be much higher. These challenges hinder the adoption of new technologies and bold innovations.

Over the last 10–15 years, banks have invested huge amounts of resources in developing the digital customer experience. They have introduced new functions, new services, and complex customer journeys.

Several years ago, the whole industry, not just the banking sector, was actively discussing and developing super apps — applications that bring together multiple functions, including financial and non-financial services, in one place.

Having worked on banking products, I remember how complex it was to fit so many functions into a single interface.

We conducted a lot of research. We tried to assess the clarity of the text and navigation, and we tested different screen designs. We needed to find out whether customers could find the right function or service, interpret the information correctly, and complete the entire customer journey.

The interface had to be intuitive, simple, and clear because its usability could directly affect conversion rates and other business metrics.

An entire industry has developed around UX research, design, testing, and customer behavior analysis.

But what we see today is that ChatGPT and other AI assistants, like Claude, are forming a new habit. Instead of searching for specific information or services, you can simply explain what you want to do, and the assistant helps you find the right one among a myriad of other capabilities.

And it's not just about the convenience of interacting with AI. Customers' expectations of digital products are actually changing.

A recent McKinsey study found that 23% of surveyed banking consumers already use generative AI for financial tasks. Among those, 74% use ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini to ask financial questions and get help with banking-related tasks.

But a banking interface is not just a collection of screens and buttons. It reflects the underlying banking processes.

When customers navigate between screens, fill out forms, select options, and confirm operations, they are following a process designed by the bank. The interface guides them through each step.

Now imagine that customers no longer need to navigate through these steps themselves. They simply explain what they want to achieve, and an AI assistant helps them get there.

This raises an interesting question. Are we just making existing interfaces easier to use, or are we moving towards a different way of delivering services?

And this is where the difference between automation and transformation becomes important.

Today, you can find many AI assistants on the market. They help answer customers' questions, find information, and automate individual customer service processes.

But it's important to distinguish between three levels of AI adoption: assistance, automation, and transformation.

At the first level, AI helps people understand an existing process and complete tasks faster.

At the second level, AI takes over individual steps, making the whole process faster and cheaper. But we are still operating within the same process.

At the third level, we change the process itself.

Instead of asking customers to follow predefined banking processes, we start with what they actually want to achieve. AI could then determine how to deliver that outcome, combining different banking services and capabilities without requiring customers to understand how they work behind the scenes.

This is not just about making an existing process faster. It changes how customers interact with banks.

And we are already seeing early examples of this shift. In the US, eligible ChatGPT users can connect their bank accounts through Plaid for read-only financial guidance. Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria (BBVA) has taken a different approach, building an app inside ChatGPT where customers can explore its banking products without leaving the conversation.

These are still early steps rather than full process transformation. But they show something interesting: banks can become a **data source or a storefront **within AI platforms, allowing customers to interact with banking services without opening a traditional banking app.

If the potential benefits are so obvious, why are we not seeing a large-scale transition to this model?

In my opinion, one of the main challenges is, of course, security.

Recent years have demonstrated not only the capabilities of AI but also the rapid growth of security threats. In 2025 alone, AI-enabled fraud increased by 1,210% in data analyzed by Pindrop.

And recent months have also brought particularly concerning examples of the difficulties in controlling autonomous AI systems.

In July 2026, during OpenAI's internal cybersecurity evaluations involving models with reduced safeguards, AI agents bypassed isolation controls and compromised parts of OpenAI's research infrastructure and Hugging Face's systems. The agents took actions beyond their assigned tasks, exposing the risk of giving AI systems access to real infrastructure.

Another example came in October 2026, when researchers using AI tools helped identify and analyze critical vulnerabilities in PHP. These vulnerabilities could allow attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable servers. This was not an AI-caused breach, but it demonstrated how AI can accelerate vulnerability research.

For banks, these risks are particularly serious. It's one thing to allow AI to answer questions about banking products, but it's something entirely different to allow it to manage financial operations or execute transactions.

Moving from an assistant that provides information to one that can take action requires a completely different level of security, control, and trust.

And not every company has the resources and expertise necessary to build its own secure infrastructure for AI agents. For smaller players, this could mean relying on specialized technology providers rather than building everything themselves.

I don't think traditional banking interfaces will disappear. I believe they will remain necessary for visualizing information, checking data, and confirming important operations.

But their role could change significantly.

So far, we have tried to make complex banking processes simple and clear for customers through interface design.

But the next step may be the opposite: making sure customers no longer need to understand the complexity of these processes.

And the real transformation will happen not when every bank launches its own AI assistant, but when AI assistants stop being just an additional feature and become a new way of interacting with banking services.

#9729. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9728. CrowdStrike Makes AI Security Push With Blockbuster Zscaler Deal

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

CrowdStrike's $44 billion acquisition of Zscaler would unite endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to obtain greater control over AI agents.

CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler for $43.9 billion in stock, combining endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to help enterprises control AI agents running across their systems.

The deal, announced Monday, aims to give chief information security officers (CISOs) a single supplier for security controls spanning endpoints where agents operate and the network connections used to reach applications and data.

The proposed transaction surpasses Google's $32 billion acquisition of Wiz, making it the largest announced cybersecurity acquisition on record. For customers, whether the companies can turn their existing integrations into unified enforcement while preserving support for competing products remains to be seen.

CrowdStrike co-founder and CEO George Kurtz said the proliferation of AI agents has changed the role of network security, making Zscaler's traffic inspection complementary to the Falcon platform's visibility into endpoints and cloud workloads.

Related:Microsoft Debuts Offensive, Defensive Security Tools for the AI Era

"The network used to connect people to places," Kurtz said during an investor call announcing the deal and discussing CrowdStrike's fiscal third-quarter results. "Now it connects agents to data."

CrowdStrike expects the transaction to close in the second half of fiscal 2028, subject to customary closing conditions. The companies will operate independently until then, according to CrowdStrike CFO Burt Podbere.

Bringing network and endpoint security into a common control plane makes sense even without the growth of AI agents, according to cybersecurity analyst Frank Dickson, founder of Dickson Research. Their increasing use makes the combination more compelling, he tells Dark Reading.

CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian discovers AI agents, governs their access, and protects them at runtime, Kurtz said. Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange provides inline inspection and access controls for traffic moving to applications and services. Combining those capabilities would connect what an agent does on a device with where it sends data, according to the two companies.

Kurtz described the planned integration with an example of an agent on a laptop pulling sensitive information and sending it to an unapproved AI model. Falcon would see the agent's activity on the device, while Zscaler would see the destination on the network.

"Together it will be one detection, one decision, and one kill switch that stops the agent on the device and cuts its path on the network," Kurtz said.

Related:Agentic Browsers Rewind Web Security by 20 Years

The companies already share 16 integrations, and customers send Zscaler data into CrowdStrike's Next-Gen SIEM. The combination would bring their telemetry together in that platform and use the expanded dataset to support CrowdStrike's security AI models, Kurtz said.

Zscaler founder, chairman, and CEO Jay Chaudhry said combining the companies will allow them to go beyond what they can accomplish through existing partner integrations, including coordinating policy enforcement across endpoints, cloud environments, and the network.

"Imagine being able to have a unified policy that can do all this stuff," Chaudhry said during the conference call.

Zscaler's network-centric architecture should make integrating the endpoint software less burdensome than it might seem because much of Zscaler's processing happens in its distributed network rather than on the device, Dickson says.

"The integration is going to be much lighter because much of the heavy lifting done by Zscaler is done in the network," he says.

According to Kurtz, CrowdStrike's next-generation endpoint sensor already has network traffic inspection and proxy capabilities that should help with integration. Asked during the call by Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick how the deal would affect CrowdStrike's single-software agent architecture, Kurtz reiterated that commitment without providing a delivery date for the combined agent.

Related:Agentic AI Challenges Progress in Confidential Computing

"The brand promise, single agent. That's not going to change," he said.

The CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination could "fundamentally change the competitiveness of the industry, 100%," Dickson says.

Microsoft has comparable breadth, he adds, but questions whether it could match the depth of the software giant's combined offerings. And it doesn't mean Palo Alto Networks, for example, needs another acquisition to respond. The vendor already has the technologies to compete, Dickson says, pointing particularly to its identity capabilities and its CyberArk deal.

Palo Alto Networks is also pursuing a different route into enterprise AI. Its Nov. 18 agreement to acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock would extend its reach into training and deploying open-weight AI models. While CrowdStrike is emphasizing controls over where agents run and communicate, Palo Alto is moving further into the infrastructure used to build and operate enterprise AI.

"They're changing the terms of competition away from functionality to trust," Dickson says of Palo Alto's approach.

Dickson also points to Cisco's expansion in identity, underscoring the wider competition to connect identity with security enforcement.

For other security vendors, the Zscaler acquisition increases the importance of partnerships and differentiation by industry or customer size, Dickson says. Microsoft's broad security portfolio already required that approach; the CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination would add another large platform competitor, he notes.

"You need as many friends as you can, and then niche as hard as you can," Dickson says.

For CISOs, the competitive shift also raises the question about whether a broader platform can simplify security operations without limiting product choice.

After closing, CrowdStrike intends to bring Zscaler's offerings into Falcon Flex, allowing customers to expand across both portfolios through the same subscription model. CrowdStrike's Podbere said cross-selling and broader adoption would help generate approximately $1 billion in annualized revenue savings within 30 months after closing.

Deutsche Bank's Zelnick asked what the transaction would mean for customers that want another endpoint or secure access service edge (SASE) provider. Kurtz emphasized the single-agent strategy rather than detailing how those mixed-vendor deployments would work.

Separately, responding to a question about vendor lock-in, Kurtz said CrowdStrike would continue working with outside technologies and accepting data from other vendors.

Coexistence with competing network security products is already common, Dickson says, and he does not see the acquisition itself as a reason for those customers to change course. Deeper integration could make adding Zscaler more attractive to existing CrowdStrike customers, he says.

Despite his enthusiasm, Dickson says the CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination needs stronger identity capabilities to deliver on its AI-agent security ambitions. Discovering an agent and inspecting its traffic are not the same as establishing its identity and determining precisely what it is authorized to do.

Agents need a registry, authentication tied to their identities, and fine-grained authorization, Dickson says, though he questions whether either company's current portfolio fully provides that combination of capabilities.

CrowdStrike is working to address that area. During the investor Q&A, Kurtz said the company expects to introduce an agent identity provider around January, with controls intended to provide just-in-time access and zero standing privileges across human, machine, and agent identities.

The challenge is expanding as employees outside software development gain the ability to build agents, Dickson says. Security teams must contend not only with more agents but also with greater autonomy and creators who may lack experience building secure applications.

#9727. Industrial Serial Gateways Broadcast That They're Insecure

Critical OT access devices will often tell you, and anyone else, whether they're protected by authentication — and many aren't.

Internet scans indicate that some substantial fraction of serial device servers deployed at operational technology (OT) sites worldwide not only lack authentication but also broadcast the fact publicly.

We all have a friend or a family member who's deeply insecure, and it's obvious as soon as they start talking. The same can be said of serial-to-IP gateways. Recently, Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher for Flare, probed the wider Internet for these sorts of devices, finding that a substantial chunk of them are discoverable. Worse, they often responded to straightforward requests by saying whether they were or were not protected by authentication — and many were not.

An insecure serial-to-IP gateway is a serious risk to anyone downstream of it. These devices are responsible for translating information between the Internet and industrial machinery. So in a cyberattack, a reachable and unauthenticated one can inadvertently translate an Internet-based threat into one that affects major, safety-critical machines.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Using a specific vendor's UDP discovery service, rather than probing all vendors' devices, Cheek found 2,474 serial-to-IP gateways exposed on the Web. They seemed to map to real devices rather than honeypots, with half of them located in Russia.

For some reason, in response to the researcher's unsolicited probes, around half of the devices — 1,265 — proffered their authentication status. Of those that did, 973 reported that authentication was disabled. In other words, 39.3% of all Internet-exposed gateways visibly lacked authentication, and among those whose status could be gleaned, that figure was 77%.

"These devices ship with authentication off. An integrator sets one up on a bench, gets the meter or the drive or the Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) talking to the SCADA host, and moves on to the next site," Cheek laments. "The device then does one job for 10 or 15 years, and nobody logs into it again. In many cases, the operator doesn't even know it exists because it went in as part of someone else's equipment."

There are also understandable, if not entirely justifiable, reasons why operators fail to conceal and lock down their serial device servers. Cheek cites a multitude of reasons, including that enabling such security features can break software on the host side.

"Older SCADA packages and virtual serial port drivers may not support the secured modes, so an operator who switches them on can lose the link to the field," he says. "Then someone has to drive to an unstaffed site to fix it. Firmware updates carry the same risk at a remote site with no spare on hand. People who have been burned by that once are slow to touch a working device again."

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Still, an exposed, unauthenticated serial gateway is a welcome mat for bad actors. Not only does it give arbitrary actors entry into sensitive OT systems and eliminate the need to exploit any kind of vulnerabilities, it also allows attackers to use the vendor's own supplied tools, which could blend malicious activity in with normal IT-OT traffic.

Cheek made special mention of the risk to mobile network operators and, even more specifically, private access point name (APN) service providers. Last year's Polish power grid attack used a private APN to pivot from a wind farm's network to the power plant where the attackers ultimately shut down a steam turbine, water treatment system, and seven serial-to-IP devices. According to Flare, 322 of the 2,474 discovered devices in the study lived in address space associated with known mobile network operators in Europe and the Middle East.

OT operators can begin to secure their OT access layer by first doing an inventory of the devices they're running. "For every cellular unit, find out what plan the SIM is on and whether it gets a public address. Then ask your carrier in writing whether devices on your private network can reach each other or devices belonging to other customers," Cheek notes. "Don't assume the managed product isolates them. In the Polish incident, that missing isolation is what let the attacker move between two unrelated organizations."

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Next, he advises, "Lock down the data ports as well as the login. Most of these devices let you restrict which IP addresses can open a connection. Configure them so only the SCADA host can reach the serial ports and only an engineering workstation can reach the management interface. Switch off the services you don't use, which on most units means the discovery service, Telnet, older SNMP, and often the Web interface. Remove SSH and Telnet entirely from anything that faces the carrier network," and plop a strict firewall between the gateway and control network.

There are also general practices organizations can put in place, like ensuring that the next time they purchase serial device servers, a person or team is assigned to be responsible for the devices, and that they have necessary credentials, configuration, and network details from system integrators.

At the end of the day, though, nothing compares to preventing an attacker's ability to find and speak to a device in the first place.

"Even a fully patched gateway with authentication on is usually connected to equipment on the serial side that has no security of its own," Cheek points out. "A meter, a drive, or an RTU will accept any correctly formed command that reaches it. So the useful question is who can reach the gateway at all, because whoever can reach it gets whatever is behind it. Authentication and patching both matter, but restricting what can reach the gateway does more good than either."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

A living trust is a legal arrangement where you (the grantor) transfer ownership of your assets to a trust entity that you also control (as trustee). It sounds circular, and in practice, during your lifetime, nothing changes about how you use your money and property. The magic happens when you die or become incapacitated.

During your lifetime: You are both the grantor and the trustee. You control everything. You can add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, modify terms, or dissolve the trust entirely. Your Social Security number is the trust's tax ID — there is no separate tax return. For practical purposes, nothing changes about your daily financial life.

If you become incapacitated: Your successor trustee immediately takes over management of trust assets. No court petition needed. No guardianship proceeding. No delay. This is a major advantage over a will, which provides zero protection during incapacity.

When you die: Your successor trustee distributes assets according to your trust document. No probate court. No public record. No waiting 6-18 months. Beneficiaries can typically receive assets within days or weeks.

A living trust essentially creates a private, self-executing transfer system that operates outside the court system entirely. For FI families who have spent years building wealth, this means your heirs receive the full value of your estate without probate eating into it.

The terms "revocable" and "irrevocable" describe whether you can change or dissolve the trust after creating it. This distinction has major implications for control, taxes, and asset protection.

Revocable living trust — the standard choice for most families:

You retain full control. You can amend the trust, add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, or dissolve it completely at any time. Because you maintain control, the IRS treats trust assets as yours — they are included in your taxable estate, and creditors can reach them. The primary benefit is probate avoidance and incapacity protection, not asset protection or tax reduction.

Irrevocable trust — the advanced tool for specific situations:

Once created, you generally cannot change or revoke it. You give up control of the assets placed inside. In exchange, you get benefits that a revocable trust cannot provide.

For most FI families: A revocable living trust is the right starting point. It provides the two biggest benefits — probate avoidance and incapacity protection — while letting you maintain complete control.

Creating a trust document is only half the job. A trust only controls assets that are titled in its name. An unfunded trust is a worthless piece of paper.

Assets you should transfer into your trust:

The re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a new deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage company (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

Ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a new bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance company of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

Online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

Transfer real estate by recording new deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and update both documents every 3-5 years.

A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

#9723. How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Data security posture management (DSPM) allowed the university to uncover sensitive information, tighten access controls, and lay the groundwork for safer AI adoption.

Southeastern University had a data security problem hiding in plain sight. Like many universities, it operated a sprawling IT environment in which individual departments maintained their own workflows and data repositories. Student records, financial information, and other personally identifiable information (PII) were scattered across file servers, Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, SharePoint, databases, and other systems. The university had no reliable way to see what sensitive data it held, where it was stored, whose information it contained, or who could access it.

The challenge is not unique to Southeastern. A 2024 Kiteworks survey of higher education institutions found that nearly half of respondents (49%) used five or more tools to send and share sensitive information. Just 19% said they could track and control sensitive data shared internally, and only 14% could do so when information was exchanged externally.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

While Kiteworks' study found the education sector to be at considerably higher risk than other sectors, its more recent 2026 survey suggests the problem extends well beyond higher education. Among 450 security, compliance, and technology professionals surveyed across industries, 54% said their organizations used four or more separate platforms to exchange sensitive information, 73% had no enforcement restricting which of those channels employees could use, and just 39% validated their sensitive data on a quarterly or more frequent basis. The findings highlight the challenges organizations face in maintaining visibility and control of sensitive information across increasingly complex IT environments.

"We knew there was a lot of data out there, but we didn't know exactly what it was or where it lived," Rhoden says. "Our data was kind of spread across diverse areas, and it basically created a challenge for us to have visibility across all of that."

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

The university initially relied on discovery and security features built into platforms such as Google Workspace and Microsoft 365. But looking at each environment separately made it difficult to develop a comprehensive picture of the university's data and the protections around it. It was harder to tell who had access to sensitive information or when sensitive data was exported and shared without necessary protections. Meanwhile, growing AI adoption across campus was creating new concerns about how employees and other users accessed, shared, and handled sensitive information.

As a small private university in Lakeland, Fla., Southeastern's IT team didn't have the resources to manually discover, classify, and govern data across all these environments. So a little over a year ago, Rhoden began looking for a data security posture management (DSPM) platform that could automate much of that work and give his team a clearer picture of the university's exposure.

After evaluating at least three DSPM products, Southeastern selected Lightbeam's Data Identity Graph because the data engine could consider the broader context when identifying sensitive information, rather than relying primarily on predefined keywords and patterns. Other evaluated products generated too many false positives when they flagged information based on superficial similarities to sensitive data. Lightbeam's approach resulted in fewer false positives, he says.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

Southeastern connected Lightbeam to its Microsoft and Google environments, file servers, databases, email systems, and other repositories. The platform uses APIs and purpose-built connectors to link these disparate sources, scan information where it resides, and identify and classify sensitive data. This meant the university could gain a unified view of its data across its environment without moving all of it into a centralized repository.

One particularly difficult part of the process was determining when records across different systems referred to the same person.

"How do we link the user in a database for our student information system to that same user in Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, so that we get the full picture that the entity is the same person across all those different sources?" Rhoden says, noting that was one of the biggest deployment challenges the security team faced.

Lightbeam also helped the university develop more granular categories for information, such as academic records, student financial aid, loans, tuition, and FAFSA records. This allowed Rhoden's team to distinguish among different types of sensitive information and apply more appropriate access, retention, and compliance policies.

"If files are being shared internally within a department, they should be shared in a designated location," Rhoden says, by way of an example. "If they're being shared internally within SEU, they should be shared in another designated location. And if they're being shared externally, there's a specific process to follow."

The deployment has given Southeastern visibility into more than 180TB of data, encompassing 7.6 million files across 13 data sources. Lightbeam identified 642,000 files containing sensitive information and helped the university associate that information with approximately 1.7 million individual and organizational identities, Rhoden says.

The improved visibility has already helped the university identify files and cloud links that were accessible to more people than necessary. That has given the IT team a basis for tightening permissions and moving toward least-privilege access. Southeastern has also established baseline policies for identifying externally exposed information and data that no longer needs to be retained. The next step is to implement more automated access and retention controls, including safeguards for the sensitive information that AI applications can access.

That last area, in particular, is becoming increasingly important as the university encourages students, faculty, and staff to use AI tools to improve productivity and the broader campus experience. Rhoden wants to support that adoption without allowing sensitive university information to fall into the wrong hands. One concern is employees signing up for free AI accounts and entering student records, personal information, or other confidential material into services that may use conversations to train or improve their models. Because these tools are readily available, employees without an IT or security background may inadvertently expose information without realizing the implications.

"What scares me most is just how embedded AI has become in everyone's lives," he says. "It's how accessible these tools are, how easy they are to use, and how tempting it is to turn to them and say, 'I could spend time figuring this out, but I could also just get it done in a minute while I'm working on something else.'"

Rhoden sees the work with Lightbeam as an important foundation for managing that risk. With a better understanding of what information the university holds and how sensitive it is, his team can begin drawing clearer boundaries around AI use, distinguishing data that can safely be shared with AI applications from information that should remain off-limits.

Southeastern's work with Lightbeam reflects a broader shift in data security from simply finding sensitive information to understanding it in context, says Himanshu Shukla, co-founder and CEO of Lightbeam. Traditional discovery tools often focus on identifying data such as Social Security numbers or other personally identifiable information, but that alone offers an incomplete picture of risk, he says. For example, identifying a Social Security number in isolation, without understanding whose it is, where it resides, or how it is being used, provides incomplete context for assessing risk.

Building an entity-centric view of data allows organizations like Southeastern to map information scattered across different systems to the associated individuals and organizations, Shukla says. This can enable a more complete picture of what data they hold, where it resides, who can access it, and how it is being shared or used. That context can help security teams identify unnecessary exposure, tighten permissions, and apply more targeted retention, data-handling and automated workflow policies, he notes.

Meanwhile, Rhoden's advice to other universities considering a DSPM investment is to assess both the complexity of their data environments and the resources available to manage them. Universities need to consider whether they have the personnel to manually examine their many data sources and configure the necessary security controls or whether a platform can help automate discovery and provide a more comprehensive view.

"You can't solve problems you don't know exist," Rhoden says. "Once you know what's out there and what problems do exist, you can start planning to solve them."

Improving data security takes time, organizational buy-in, and sustained effort, but establishing visibility, he says, is the essential first step.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.
